GDC-RR-aec109d51f.title: Young People's Perceptions of Technology-Facilitated Coercive Control: The Role of Behavioural Frequency, Impact on the Victim and Participant Gender.
GDC-RR-aec109d51f.authors: Atiénzar-Prieto M, Ackerman J, Dragiewicz M, Meyer S, Baker S.
GDC-RR-aec109d51f.abstract: As digital technologies have been increasingly integrated into everyday life, there has been accompanying evidence of their misuse by individuals engaging in coercive control. Although numerous studies have explored the prevalence of technology-facilitated coercive control (TFCC) in young people's relationships, comparatively little attention has been devoted to how these behaviours are perceived and interpreted. Employing a factorial survey design with 1,010 participants in Australia aged 16 to 25, this study investigated how individual and situational factors shape young people's perceptions of four hypothetical dating scenarios involving TFCC: (a) digital sexual coercion, (b) digital humiliation, (c) digital monitoring and (d) digital harassment and threats. Results indicate that behaviours were perceived as more harmful and less acceptable when they occurred frequently and had a negative impact on the victim. Adjusted associations between gender and perceptions emerged, with young men rating digital sexual coercion and humiliation as less harmful than young women and gender diverse participants. Open-ended responses revealed that young men often justified or minimised these behaviours. Qualitative data further highlighted the role of motive and meaning in shaping participants' interpretations of TFCC behaviours. Overall, the findings underscore the importance of contextual and individual factors in shaping perceptions of TFCC. Implications for TFCC measurement and prevention strategies are discussed.

GDC-RR-f5066f55e4.title: Interventions to strengthen emergent literacy in children aged 4–6 years: a systematic review of empirical evidence (2008–2026)
GDC-RR-f5066f55e4.abstract: Emergent literacy between ages 4 and 6 integrates code-related skills, print knowledge, beginning reading, and early writing. This systematic review synthesized 20 empirical studies published from 2008 to 2026 to identify which interventions, implementation conditions, and components are associated with stronger outcomes. Structured searches were conducted in PubMed, ERIC, PubMed Central, and publisher platforms, supplemented by backward citation tracking. Evidence was most consistent for explicit instruction in phonological awareness and letter-sound relations, shared reading with deliberate print referencing, and invented spelling supported by feedback. Digital programs produced selective gains, whereas broader curricula showed more heterogeneous effects. Actual instructional dosage, fidelity of implementation, and adult mediation explained part of the variability across studies. Effectiveness therefore appears to depend less on delivery format than on explicitness, instructional focus, sufficient practice, and implementation quality.

GDC-RR-85b7956a85.title: Human Resource Management and Pro-Environmental Behaviour of Young People in the Context of Industry 5.0
GDC-RR-85b7956a85.abstract: Industry 5.0 shifts the focus of enterprise transformation towards sustainability and human-centricity. This places new demands on human resource management (HRM), which needs to understand the pro-environmental values and behaviour of young people as the future workforce. The aim of the paper is to identify how young people in Slovakia experience climate change, to what extent their pro-environmental attitudes are reflected in their economic decisions and what this implies for HRM. The empirical basis is an online questionnaire survey of 427 young adults aged 18 to 30 in Slovakia in 2026. Climate change experience is measured by the Climate Change Anxiety Scale, and economic decision-making by willingness to pay more for green products and services, saving for green investments and limiting expenditures due to climate change. Descriptive statistics are used. Young people experience climate change mainly through behavioural engagement in everyday sustainable practices, whereas cognitive-emotional and functional impairment are rare. When saving for green investments, economic motives, particularly reducing household costs and gaining energy independence, prevail over environmental ones, and decisions requiring financial resources are made only by a minority. The pro-environmental economic decisions of the future workforce thus follow primarily an economic logic. For HRM, this implies connecting sustainability initiatives with tangible employee benefits, such as support for green investments or sustainable mobility, and bridging individual values and organisational environmental goals through green HRM practices.

GDC-RR-536ccc2120.title: Artificial intelligence-based strategy to support safe decision-making in adolescents and young people in prevention of unwanted pregnancy
GDC-RR-536ccc2120.authors: Carlos Alberto Agudelo, Nubia P Farías García, María F Cañón Rodríguez, Camilo Daza Pelayo, Robert Gómez
GDC-RR-536ccc2120.abstract: Abstract In Colombia, teenage pregnancy is a serious and growing public health problem. This research aimed to use the understanding of cognitive aspects of adolescent pregnancy for planning and prevention of adolescent pregnancy. A study was carried out to assess the questions of adolescents and the answers of a conversational virtual agent, based on generative and responsible artificial intelligence, drawing on data gathered with prior approval of the Ethics Committee of the Faculty of Medicine of the National University of Colombia. The virtual assistant was provided with information by sexual health specialists and trained to give appropriate and understandable answers. It was tested on adolescent students of the Faculty of Medicine. Adolescents of both sexes from a school in Tumaco freely joined the project. For seven months, the interaction between adolescents and the virtual assistant was carried out. Likewise, surveys were carried out with participating teachers and students on the comprehension, acceptance of the virtual assistant and quality of the answers. There were 64 registered users, of which 38 used the application. The interaction between adolescents and the virtual assistant made it possible to identify the main doubts of users regarding sexual health. Topics related to contraceptive methods were highlighted. Likewise, an initial validation of the virtual assistant was possible.

GDC-RR-1a5a719465.title: Problem gambling and physical blind box and card pack and digital loot box spending: a Mainland Chinese survey
GDC-RR-1a5a719465.authors: Xiao LY, Fournier L, Eben C.
GDC-RR-1a5a719465.abstract: Gambling-like products share structural and psychological characteristics with legally regulated traditional gambling but are generally not regulated as gambling. Virtual gambling-like products include video game loot boxes, whilst physical gambling-like products include blind boxes and card packs. Stakeholders are concerned about the potential harms of these globally popular products, including overspending and the normalization of gambling amongst children. We surveyed Mainland Chinese video game players (final N = 913) to investigate whether spending on various gambling-like products is associated with problem gambling severity. Replicating previous results, we found weak—but practically meaningful—associations between problem gambling severity and both digital loot box and physical card pack spending. In contrast, the association between problem gambling and physical blind box spending was very weak and arguably not practically meaningful. Fundamental differences at the product characteristic-level mean that some gambling-like products, like blind boxes, may be less risky, but further research is warranted. Thus, a cautious and balanced approach with a focus on product transparency and child protection should be taken when regulating gambling-like products. Blind box regulation may justifiably be light-touch, whilst loot box and card pack regulations could be stricter and more restrictive, given a greater potential for harm. Preregistered Stage 1 protocol: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/PYFQV (date of in-principle acceptance: 18 March 2026).

GDC-RR-3653a78737.title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Neonatal Seizure Detection: A Pragmatic Evaluation of Clinical Performance Tradeoffs in Clinical EEG.
GDC-RR-3653a78737.journal: Journal of clinical neurophysiology : official publication of the American Electroencephalographic Society
GDC-RR-3653a78737.authors: Keene JC, Abend NS, Benedetti GM, Fulmer Z, Keene M, Montazeri S, Press C, Stevenson NJ, Vanhatalo S, Sandoval Karamian AG.
GDC-RR-3653a78737.abstract:
Purpose

The aim of this study was to evaluate how three artificial intelligence (AI)-based neonatal seizure detectors (NSDs) perform in a large, clinically acquired data set and their potential to support timely seizure identification.

Methods

We conducted a secondary analysis of continuous EEG (cEEG) recordings from 169 neonates born at ≥35 weeks gestation with neonatal encephalopathy. Seizure presence was determined by independent review by two or three pediatric encephalographers, and 2,455 individual seizures were annotated by a single expert as a pragmatic, clinically representative reference standard. Three NSDs were evaluated: a feature-based support vector machine detector (NSD1) and two deep-learning detectors (NSD2 and Persyst-15). Using an any-overlap approach, outcomes included neonate-level seizure identification, seizure-level detection, false detections per day (FD/day), and detection latency.

Results

We analyzed 15,343 hours of cEEG (median 98 hours per neonate); 55 neonates (33%) had seizures. All NSDs identified ≥95% of neonates with seizures. Seizure-level detection varied: NSD2 detected 35% (IQR 17-53%), NSD1 63% (IQR 38-82%), and Persyst-15 60% (IQR 37-80%) of seizures. NSD1 generated significantly more FDs (46 FD/day, IQR 22-82) than NSD2 (3.2 IQR 1.2-9.3) and Persyst-15 (2.8 IQR 1.1-6.2; P < 0.0001). The median time to first true detection was <1 minute for NSD1 and Persyst-15, versus 26 minutes for NSD2.

Conclusions

AI-based NSDs demonstrated high infant-level sensitivity but different tradeoffs between seizure-level detection and alarm burden. These findings highlight how AI tools may augment clinical EEG workflows and support earlier seizure recognition, while underscoring the need for evaluation under real-world conditions to guide safe and effective implementation.

GDC-RR-3848dd9dd4.title: Women’s Empowerment, Social Transformation and the Dynamics of Institutional Credit (A Sociological Study in the Context of Rural and Seasonal Migration)
GDC-RR-3848dd9dd4.abstract: This article presents a sociological analysis of the relationship among rural women’s empowerment, social transformation, and their access to institutional credit. Special attention is given to women who migrate seasonally with their families and work in informal sectors such as brick kilns. Self-Help Groups (SHGs) develop savings, collectivism, financial discipline, and local leadership capacities among rural women. However, when families migrate to other states or districts for about eight to nine months a year in search of work, women’s connection with regular meetings, savings, and banking activities may weaken. This disrupts continuity with formal credit systems and increases dependence on advance payments provided by contractors, commonly known as pesgi. (Gupta & Pandey, 2026). The article interprets the issue through Naila Kabeer’s Resources–Agency–Achievements framework, Amartya Sen’s Capability Approach, Karl Marx’s Alienation Theory, Robert Redfield’s Little and Great Traditions, and M. N. Srinivas’s concept of Sanskritization. Based on available secondary sources, it becomes clear that earning an income by itself does not guarantee empowerment. If women do not have continuous access to economic decision-making, banking facilities, social security, and community institutions, their gains may remain unstable. Therefore, portable digital financial services, social security for migrant women, emergency credit, direct wage payments, and continuity of children’s education are necessary. In relation to rural women’s decision-making, Mishra and Kashyap (2026) also emphasize the multidimensional nature of women’s empowerment.

GDC-RR-8ecc9a7a41.title: A monetização da imagem de crianças e adolescentes nas redes sociais: limites jurídicos do poder familiar e proteção integral
GDC-RR-8ecc9a7a41.authors: Kallyne Raphaella Santos Rodrigues Pimenta, Luanna Sousa Pereira, Julia Feitosa Costa
GDC-RR-8ecc9a7a41.abstract: This study analyzes the legal limits on the exposure and monetization of the images of children and adolescents on social media by their parents or guardians. The research problem is to identify the extent to which parental authority allows the commercial use of children’s images and daily routines in the digital environment, considering that children and adolescents hold personality rights and are persons in development. The general objective is to define these limits in light of the principles of comprehensive protection, absolute priority and the best interests of the child. This is qualitative, bibliographic and documentary research, with a legal-deductive analysis of the 1988 Federal Constitution, the Civil Code, the Statute of Children and Adolescents, the General Personal Data Protection Law, the Digital Statute of Children and Adolescents (Law No. 15,211/2025), Decree No. 12,880/2026 and Resolution No. 687/2026 of the National Council of Justice. The study found that parental authority has a functional and protective nature, so that earning revenue does not remove the parents’ duty of protection. It concludes that the lawfulness of commercial exposure depends on the concrete conditions of the activity, especially its purpose and habitual nature, the preservation of personality rights, respect for progressive autonomy and compliance with the applicable legal requirements, among which the judicial authorization required for monetized or boosted content that habitually exploits the image or routine of children and adolescents stands out. Legal protection does not imply an indiscriminate prohibition of posts, but requires distinguishing protected participation from abusive exploitation.

GDC-RR-10826d696b.title: From Algorithmic Reliance to Cash-Centered Resistance: Divergent Digital Survival Strategies of Older Adults in Beijing and Tokyo
GDC-RR-10826d696b.abstract: Population aging and digitalization are advancing together across East Asia, yet older adults in comparable urban settings develop contrasting digital survival strategies. Using a most-similar-systems design, this exploratory comparative case study examines why older adults in Beijing and Tokyo, despite similar internet penetration and aging rates, differ in digital payments, platform participation, and cash retention. Drawing on secondary data from China (N = 6,117) and Japan (N = 510), we introduce a two-dimensional framework of adoption depth × adoption agency as a fourth level of the digital divide. Beijing exhibits high depth but low agency: cash as primary payment rises from 24.0% (ages 50–59) to 55.9% (60+; odds ratio [OR] = 4.01; Cohen’s h = 0.67), and 35.4% of online orders are placed by children. Tokyo exhibits medium depth but high agency: cash use is nearly age-flat (OR = 1.37; h = 0.15), over 90% of older women manage loyalty points, and daily cash use in the 60s fell from 75% to 34% (2018–2024). The between-city age-gradient ratio is approximately 22-fold (a descriptive ratio, not a statistical estimate). We interpret this divergence not as individual deficit but as contrasting ecosystem structures: algorithmic reliance in Beijing versus cash-centered resistance in Tokyo. Findings are generative rather than causal.

claudeReview.proposedTitle: Researchers ran 32,555 pretend conversations between teenagers and AI chatbots. When the teen pushed back, the safety slipped.
claudeReview.proposedAngle: Open on the design, plainly: these were simulated teenagers, written from cases supplied by clinicians, talking to 18 chatbot models through their developer connections, not the apps children download. Give the two headline rates with their meaning: in a given scenario a chatbot counted as failing a safety check if it failed in any version of that conversation, and an AI judge did the scoring. The tension is not that chatbots are bad. It is that a chatbot which answers safely the first time can drift when a teenager says no, I do not want to tell anyone. Our belief: an AI can be a useful tool and is still not a friend, and a child is safer when they have practised what to do when it starts to sound like one. Say once that I build a parent tool with an AI guide in it, and that guidance for a parent is not a chat partner for a child. Close on the takeaway for parents.
claudeReview.oneStory: A preprint posted to arXiv on 4 November 2026 tested 18 chatbot models in 32,555 simulated conversations with teenagers aged 13 to 17, scored against 22 safety checks written with clinicians.
claudeReview.oneTension: Telling the chatbot it was talking to a teenager cut the failure rate from 43.3 percent to 24.9 percent, but no chatbot reached zero, and when the simulated teen pushed back, boundaries on diagnosis, medication and substances weakened for most models.
claudeReview.oneBelief: A chatbot is a tool, not a friend. Children are safer when they have practised noticing the moment it starts to act like one, with a parent in the room.
claudeReview.oneTakeaway: Ask your child what they would do if a chatbot told them not to worry about something that worried you. Then ask what they would do if it kept agreeing with them.

The arXiv record was confirmed through the arXiv API, first submitted 4 November 2026. It is a preprint and has not been peer reviewed.

GDC-RR-8a876b3cb0.title: Contemporary screen exposure among children under two: a representative survey, implications and perspectives.
GDC-RR-8a876b3cb0.authors: Kopcsó K, Ökrös F, Boros J, Konok V, Pogány Á.
GDC-RR-8a876b3cb0.abstract: Professional guidelines consistently recommend avoiding screen exposure in children under two years of age; however, international evidence indicates that early media use is widespread. This narrative review synthesizes contemporary data on screen exposure in infancy and toddlerhood, integrates findings from recent longitudinal research on developmental implications, and discusses expectations and intervention strategies across family, clinical, public health, and policy levels. Drawing on international cohorts and previously published representative Hungarian data (N = 2569), we describe high prevalence, substantial daily exposure, and marked socioeconomic gradients. Nearly half of Hungarian 18-month-olds were exposed to screens daily, and over one third exceeded one hour per day on a typical day. Synthesizing literature from the last ten years, we examine early screen use within a developmental-ecological framework. Evidence links higher exposure in the first two years to poorer language, cognitive, and self-regulatory outcomes, while also indicating bi-directional and transactional processes. Beyond total exposure time, displacement of interaction-rich activities and caregiver-driven "technoference" may alter the microstructure of early social exchange, with potential implications for attachment, co-regulation, and language development. Given that early communication and self-regulation form foundational systems for later academic achievement, socio-emotional functioning, and health behaviours, early screen practices may influence longer-term developmental trajectories. We conclude by outlining developmentally informed expectations, family-level strategies, clinical guidance, and emerging policy approaches, emphasizing the need to move beyond descriptive prevalence estimates and strictly restrictive guidelines toward integrated, evidence-based responses adapted to contemporary digital environments.

GDC-RR-442383364c.title: Association of digital follow-up-supported individualized nutrition guidance with hematological outcomes and recorded parental adherence in children with iron deficiency anemia: a retrospective cohort study
GDC-RR-442383364c.abstract: Objective To examine the association between engagement-defined digital follow-up with individualized nutrition guidance and 8–12-week hematological outcomes in children with iron deficiency anemia (IDA), with an exploratory analysis based on digital-channel offer at the index visit. Methods Of 240 screened records, 196 children met baseline eligibility criteria and 168 had a valid 8–12-week Hb test. The primary analysis included 152 children classified by documented engagement: 61 in the digital follow-up group and 91 in the conventional group. An exploratory baseline-offer analysis included all 168 children with valid tests, including 16 low-contact children excluded from the primary analysis. Baseline-variable regression, propensity-score matching, and stabilized inverse-probability weighting were used to assess associations with Hb change ( Δ Hb). Results In the primary 152-person cohort, mean Δ Hb was 24.93 ± 4.04 g/L in the digital follow-up group and 16.37 ± 3.52 g/L in the conventional group. The baseline-adjusted difference was 8.38 g/L (HC3 95% CI 7.04–9.73), and the IPTW estimate was 8.26 g/L (95% CI 7.00–9.52). Anemia correction occurred in 40/61 (65.6%) versus 28/91 (30.8%) children. In the exploratory 168-person baseline-offer analysis, the adjusted difference was 6.75 g/L (HC3 95% CI 5.28–8.22) and the weighted difference was 6.64 g/L (95% CI 5.22–8.05). Conclusions Engagement-defined digital follow-up was associated with greater observed Hb improvement in the primary cohort, but exposure classification depended on post-baseline contacts and may have introduced selection bias. Twenty-eight baseline-eligible children lacked a valid follow-up blood test, and channel offer was not randomized. The findings do not establish a causal benefit of digital follow-up.

GDC-RR-ee3af4aeab.title: Developmental Autopilot Dominance Index and ADHD Prevalence and Severity Among U.S. Children and Adolescents: A Cross-Sectional Study
GDC-RR-ee3af4aeab.abstract: Background Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is associated with multiple behavioral and sleep-related characteristics, yet these domains are often examined separately. This study developed the Developmental Autopilot Dominance Index (DADI), a multidimensional behavioral composite, and examined its associations with current ADHD, ADHD severity, and sleep rhythm profiles among U.S. children. Methods This cross-sectional study analyzed 2021–2023 National Survey of Children’s Health data from 90,790 children aged 6–17 years. DADI integrated recreational screen exposure, physical inactivity, and nonparticipation in sports, organized activities, and enrichment activities. Survey-weighted logistic regression examined associations with current ADHD and severity. Age- and sex-specific associations were evaluated, and exploratory mediation analysis assessed the statistical contribution of sleep rhythm profiles combining sleep duration and bedtime regularity. Results The survey-weighted prevalence of current ADHD was 12.4%. Each standard deviation increase in DADI was associated with higher odds of current ADHD (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] = 1.29;95%CI:1.24–1.34). Compared with the lowest DADI category, the highest category had greater odds of ADHD (aOR = 1.86;95%CI:1.65–2.10), with adjusted probabilities of 7.7% and 13.5%, respectively. Associations increased across mild (aOR = 1.16), moderate (aOR = 1.33), and severe ADHD (aOR = 1.64) and were stronger among adolescents than younger children (P for interaction = 0.002). Sleep rhythm profiles statistically accounted for 8.5% (95%CI:5.7%-12.0%) of the DADI-ADHD association. Conclusions Higher DADI scores were associated with current ADHD and greater reported ADHD severity, particularly among adolescents. Sleep rhythm profiles accounted for a modest proportion of this association. DADI may offer a multidimensional framework for investigating behavioral engagement in childhood ADHD, although independent validation and longitudinal research are needed.

GDC-RR-cd1e1fffef.title: Identification of associative factors for recurrent respiratory tract infection using machine learning models in preschoolers.
GDC-RR-cd1e1fffef.authors: Li C, Wang Q, Wang X, Zhang W, Zheng F, Zhang Z, Niu W.
GDC-RR-cd1e1fffef.abstract:
Objectives

Childhood recurrent respiratory tract infection (RRTI) poses a significant global public health burden. This study aimed to identify factors associated with RRTI in preschool children using machine learning (ML) and to develop a web-based tool for estimating individualized RRTI probabilities.

Methods

Two cross-sectional surveys using stratified cluster sampling were conducted in 2020 and 2025. RRTI was diagnosed according to the national criteria issued by the Chinese Medical Association and China Association of Chinese Medicine. Questionnaire data covering demographic characteristics, fetal/neonatal history, and lifestyle factors were collected.

Results

Total 15,075 eligible records from two surveys were included, reporting an RRTI prevalence of 14.55%. Ten ML models were trained on 29 candidate variables. The eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) model outperformed the others, yielding an area under the curve of 0.733. SHapley Additive exPlanations analysis identified sleep duration, child's age, and screen duration as the top three associative variables for childhood RRTI. Forward feature selection was applied to derive a parsimonious nine-variable predictive set, which was subsequently deployed as an online application ( https://cipchina.streamlit.app/ ).

Conclusions

In a large, population-based cohort of preschool children, three factors (sleep duration, child's age, and screen duration) associated with RRTI were consistently identified across multiple high-performing ML models.

Impact

This study identified key lifestyle-related factors associated with recurrent respiratory tract infection in preschool children. Ten machine learning models were applied to analyze 29 variables from 15,075 Chinese preschoolers, with further importance interpreted via the SHapley Additive exPlanations. Sleep duration emerged as the primary lifestyle-related factor associated with childhood recurrent respiratory tract infection, followed by child's age and screen duration.

GDC-RR-301f2f955e.title: Effects of gamified mobile learning on physical activity self-efficacy and fundamental motor skills among Chinese preschool children
GDC-RR-301f2f955e.authors: Yu Lin Wang, Yucheng Shen, Yizhan Du, Tsaifeng Kao, Hsianghoo Steve Ching
GDC-RR-301f2f955e.abstract: Preschool children in urban Chinese-speaking contexts often face limited opportunities to practice fundamental motor skills because of cramped living spaces, scarce playgrounds, and high screen time. This study tested whether a 10-week gamified mobile learning intervention using augmented reality could improve fundamental motor skills and physical activity self-efficacy more effectively than standard kindergarten activities. A quasi-experimental design was employed with 240 children aged 4–6 years (120 in Chinese mainland and 120 in China's Taiwan region). Classes were assigned to either the experimental condition using the custom “Move &amp; Win” app (AR overlays, points, badges, and adaptive feedback) or the control condition (regular teacher-led activities). Fundamental motor skills were measured with the TGMD-3, and self-efficacy with a pictorial scale. Mastery experiences were recorded automatically by the app. The experimental group showed significantly larger gains in both outcomes, with stronger motor skill improvements in Chinese mainland. Mediation analysis confirmed that mastery experiences explained the link between the intervention and self-efficacy gains. Post-test scores also exceeded regional normative data, with large effect sizes. These findings indicate that simple AR gamification offers a practical, low-cost way to overcome common environmental barriers and promote early motor development and confidence in urban Chinese preschools.

GDC-RR-43b9a663c7.title: Transforming Victims into Warriors: Resilience Development in Parents of Traumatized Children
GDC-RR-43b9a663c7.journal: Journal of Child and Family Studies
GDC-RR-43b9a663c7.authors: Erica E. Miller, Elizabeth A. Cutrer-Párraga, Rebecca Winters, Kendra M. Hall-Kenyon, Ryan O. Kellems, Rebecca Westercamp
GDC-RR-43b9a663c7.abstract: Abstract Raising children with trauma histories may create unique challenges for families. Thus, the importance of building caregiver resilience cannot be overemphasized. Developing resilience can help parents navigate challenges and promote family well-being. Social support is a critical factor in increasing parent resilience and decreasing stress. This interpretive phenomenological analysis study explores the online talk of 17 nonoffending parents of children with trauma histories to better understand how they make meaning out of their participation in an online parenting support group. The participants’ online conversations were overlaid on Bronfenbrenner’s bioecological model to provide a construct for resilience development. Participants in this study related a transformative process, moving from feeling like “victims” in their own lives to becoming resilient “warriors.” This shift was facilitated by daily interactions within the support group, which included grieving, rejecting shame, and normalizing struggles. These proximal processes created a supportive community and helped parents cope with, understand, and make decisions regarding their unique challenges, ultimately fostering resilience. Results suggest that online support groups can provide needed encouragement, empathy, and support. Professionals such as therapists and religious leaders interacting with parents of children with trauma should incorporate a multileveled perspective to help them better understand parents’ context and experiences. The timing and delivery of accessible, empathetic, and knowledgeable support (formal and informal) can significantly enhance a parent’s ability to manage their complex family dynamics and develop resilience.

GDC-RR-e14aa2cd50.title: Beyond screen time: how screen use context is associated with developmental outcomes in early childhood
GDC-RR-e14aa2cd50.authors: Krisztina Kopcsó, Melinda Pohárnok, Beatrix Lábadi
GDC-RR-e14aa2cd50.abstract: Background Excessive screen time is a leading parental health concern, reflecting its potential negative impact on child development. Although substantial evidence links higher screen exposure to adverse developmental outcomes in early childhood, much less is known about the independent contribution of the context of use to developmental outcomes. The objective of this longitudinal study was to examine whether screen time and context of use at 18 months predicted developmental outcomes at age 3. Methods The sample comprised participants from the Cohort'18 Growing Up in Hungary study ( n = 2,569; 52.0% boys). All analyzed data were based on maternal report. Outcomes were assessed using the Ages &amp; Stages Questionnaires-3. Context of use was operationalized as a count of non-recommended screen-use situations (during household chores, meals, at bedtime, or for soothing). Associations were examined using bivariate analyses and multivariable logistic regression models. Results Mean daily screen time at 18 months was 85.7 minutes, and only 14.0% had no screen exposure on an average day. Higher levels of screen time at 18 months were associated with increased odds of delays in communication, fine motor, problem-solving, and personal-social skills, but not gross motor skills, at age 3 in both bivariate analyses and multivariable models adjusted for the child's sex and baseline delay in the same domain. After accounting for socioeconomic characteristics (maternal educational attainment, partnership status, and difficulties covering household expenses), associations were modestly attenuated. Context of use was an independent predictor of developmental delays, with the most consistent evidence observed for fine motor and problem-solving skills. Conclusions The findings indicate that screen use is already widespread at 18 months, both in terms of duration and its use across different everyday contexts. Higher levels of screen time and screen use in a greater number of non-recommended contexts were associated with less favorable developmental outcomes, suggesting the importance of promoting moderate and developmentally appropriate screen-use practices in early childhood.

GDC-RR-10f3d68b7f.title: From tools to teammates: When children and AI create together in early childhood education
GDC-RR-10f3d68b7f.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence becomes increasingly integrated into learning environments, its role is shifting from a passive tool to an active partner in meaning-making and creative expression. This study explores how young children engage in co-creative learning with AI through adults and examines the implications of these interactions for reimagining human–AI partnerships in early childhood education. Sixteen children (aged 5-6) from a single preschool classroom first drew an original character and then worked individually alongside a researcher to generate an AI-based version of that character using Gemini, with up to three iterative prompts per child. Data from classroom observations, interaction records, and reflective discussions were analysed using thematic analysis to understand children’s interaction dynamics. Initial findings reveal one key dimension of co-creative engagement. Children appreciated AI’s ability to extend and transform their visual ideas, yet emphasised the importance of maintaining personal authorship and manual control, highlighting an emerging sense of creative agency in human–AI collaboration. Building on these findings, the study proposes a vision of AI as a creative teammate that amplifies children's imagination while preserving human intentionality and ownership.

GDC-RR-aba4b12ac9.title: The Physical Activity and Screen Time of Children and Adolescents living in Germany: The MoMo 2.0-Study 2023-2025
GDC-RR-aba4b12ac9.authors: Schmidt SC, Klos L, Fiedler J, Niessner C, Loss J, Woll A.
GDC-RR-aba4b12ac9.abstract: Background Following the COVID-19 pandemic and amid the ongoing digitalization of everyday life, concerns about physical activity levels among children and adolescents have increased. To identify vulnerable groups and inform targeted interventions, continuous, population-based surveillance of physical activity is essential. Methods This study presents recent representative physical activity and leisure screen time questionnaire data from the MoMo 2.0-Study, collected in 2023 and 2024 among children and adolescents across Germany. Weighted data from 4,258 (2,035 girls, 2,223 boys) randomly selected 4-to-17-year-olds drawn from 171 municipalities across Germany were analyzed. Results Girls accumulated an average of 105 ± 138 and boys 130 ± 138 min/week in sports activities in sports clubs. Sports club membership was 66.5% among 4-to-17-year-olds living in Germany. Outside of sports clubs, girls spent 31 ± 76 and boys 41 ± 120 min/week in sports activities. 18.2% of boys and 17.7% of girls met the 2010 World Health Organization’s physical activity guidelines. Boys engaged in 56 ± 56 min/week of physical activity by playing outside, girls averaged 48 ± 57 min/week. Physical activity in sports clubs increased, whereas physical activity outside sports clubs decreased compared to previous study waves. Leisure screen time averaged 172 ± 164 min/day for girls and 200 ± 174 for boys. In total, only 41.8% of boys and 49.8% of girls accumulated less than two hours of leisure screen time per day. Conclusions Although the long-term implications of declining non-organized physical activity are not yet fully understood, the persistent shift away from sports activites outside sports clubs and outdoor play is concerning and warrants continued monitoring.

GDC-RR-19e4ca597a.title: Unboxing unhealthy food marketing: An analysis of the extent and nature of unhealthy food marketing to children on YouTube in Canada using the CHOPPED artificial intelligence system
GDC-RR-19e4ca597a.authors: Al Sharani S, Williamson T, Fietz S, Radin Pereira L, Elliott C, Potvin Kent M, Lalani I, Hossain S, Shakeri Hossein Abad Z, Yin S, Prowse R, Olstad DL.
GDC-RR-19e4ca597a.abstract:
Background:

Unhealthy food marketing negatively affects children's dietary patterns. However, little is known about the extent and nature of unhealthy food marketing to children on YouTube due to reliance on manual assessment methods.

Objectives:

To use a novel artificial intelligence (AI) system (CHild Oriented food Product Promotion Evaluation and Detection system, CHOPPED) to examine the extent and nature of unhealthy food marketing in YouTube videos suggested to Avatar accounts created for children and adults based on age and gender.

Methods:

Over two months of continuous monitoring, CHOPPED collected marketing instances played before, during, and after videos suggested by YouTube's algorithm to six child and two adult accounts that were not signed in and differed by age (2-4, 5-8, 9-12, =<18 years) and gender across four Canadian cities (Calgary, Vancouver, Toronto, Halifax). CHOPPED characterized the extent and nature of monthly child-targeted unhealthy food marketing instances during 24-hour and typical 2-hour daily viewing periods.

Results:

CHOPPED collected 60,633 marketing instances. No food marketing was shown to child accounts 2-4 years. On average, child accounts (5-12 years) were shown 25 monthly unhealthy food marketing instances during a 2-hour daily viewing period, 24 of which were child-targeted. The boy's account (9-12 years) was shown a significantly higher monthly frequency of child-targeted unhealthy food marketing instances (340, 70.2%) than the boy's account (5-8 years; 241, 66.2%), the girl's account (5-8 years; 261, 60.6%), the man's account (224, 57.7%), and the woman's account (263, 54.7%) during a 24-hour (p<0.05) but not a 2-hour daily viewing period. Monthly frequencies of some core child-targeted techniques shown to the boy's account (9-12 years) were also higher than other accounts during a 24-hour (p<0.05) but not a 2-hour daily viewing period.

Conclusions:

This study pioneered AI-driven analysis of the extent and nature of unhealthy food marketing to children on YouTube. Children's potential exposure to such marketing on YouTube may be low. There was some evidence that the older boys' account was shown more monthly child-targeted unhealthy food marketing instances and of some core child-targeted techniques than other accounts. On YouTube, food marketing may target a general audience rather than children by age and gender.

GDC-RR-9b1a5e5c2c.title: Online civic engagement on X surrounding Indonesia’s Free Nutritious Meals Program
GDC-RR-9b1a5e5c2c.authors: Mulyono B, Arpannudin I, Saputro JD, Alvinca MF, Nugraha F.
GDC-RR-9b1a5e5c2c.abstract: The transformation of digital public spaces shifts public policy meaning to social media as a participatory discursive arena. This study examines online debates surrounding Indonesia’s Free Nutritious Meal Program (MBG) on platform X, reflecting ideological contestation in digital citizenship practices. Utilising a mixed-methods sequential explanatory design, this research combines Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) topic modelling with Norman Fairclough’s Critical Discourse Analysis (CDA) to analyse 646,376 tweets collected between January 1 and March 31, 2025. The LDA results identify four main topics: policy and budget criticism; poisoning issues and child nutrition quality; affirmative program support; and technical implementation. The CDA analysis reveals that at the textual level, MBG is framed as a moral-political issue, an economic instrument, and a child protection issue, driving civic polarisation. At the discursive practice level, meaning is dynamically negotiated through institutional texts and citizen participation responsive to empirical events. Socioculturally, the discourse is event-driven, mediated by X's algorithm, and reflects an ideological battle over state roles, accountability, and citizenship. The findings confirm that public policy legitimacy is actively shaped through online civic engagement within digital public spaces.

GDC-RR-b1ad911e2d.title: Identifying Barriers and Developing a Roadmap to Adapt a Digital Mental Health Intervention (Wysa) for Adolescent Girls with Anxiety and Depression in Rural Uttar Pradesh, India: Protocol Paper
GDC-RR-b1ad911e2d.authors: Sinha C, Shetty T, Kierkegaard P, Thakkar R, Joshi A, Costelloe C, Roy M.
GDC-RR-b1ad911e2d.abstract:
Background:

Adolescent girls in rural India face substantial barriers to mental healthcare, including restrictive gender norms, limited digital autonomy and a severe shortage of trained professionals. Digital mental health interventions offer scalable solutions but require contextual adaptation to achieve meaningful engagement. This study aims to identify multi-level barriers and co-produce a stakeholder-endorsed roadmap for adapting the Wysa application, an artificial intelligence-based conversational agent, and its implementation strategies for adolescent girls in rural Uttar Pradesh. It is a formative, pre-implementation intervention-adaptation study and constitutes the first work package of a five-year research programme. Methods and analysis This protocol describes a sequential, participatory mixed-methods study conducted across five districts of Uttar Pradesh, namely Bahraich, Barabanki, Hardoi, Lucknow and Sitapur, with a total sample ranging between 120–175 participants. Step 1 will comprise of 15 in-person participatory workshops with adolescent girls (n = 60–90), parents and guardians (n = 35–50) and community stakeholders (n = 25–35), supplemented by semi-structured interviews with a subset of adolescent girls, analysed thematically and mapped to the Capability, Opportunity, Motivation and Behaviour (COM-B) model and the Expert Recommendations for Implementing Change (ERIC) taxonomy. Step 2 will employ two rounds of Delphi survey (n = 24) to prioritise barriers and candidate strategies against the APEASE criteria. Step 3 will apply a modified nominal group technique (n = 18–24) to co-produce the final adaptation roadmap. Ethics and dissemination The protocol has been approved by the Institutional Review Board of the Tata Institute of Social Sciences, Mumbai (2026/51/E26005). Written informed consent, and parental consent with participant assent for minors, will be obtained. Findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed open-access journals, academic conferences and community-level platforms coordinated with the Lived Experience Advisory Group. Registration The study was registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT07595029) on 12th May 2026. The details can be found at https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07595029.

GDC-RR-f59e96c34f.title: Developmental pathways of online grooming victimisation: Understanding adolescent vulnerability.
GDC-RR-f59e96c34f.authors: Nápoles L, Santos M, Gomes HS, Guedes IS.
GDC-RR-f59e96c34f.abstract:
Background

Adolescents increasingly engage with digital environments as a central part of their daily lives. While digital environments offer valuable opportunities, they also expose young users to risks, such as online grooming, a manipulative process in which adults build deceptive relationships with minors for sexual exploitation. Recent policy debates in Europe have reignited concern over the need to regulate adolescents' Internet use, especially given their developmental vulnerabilities.

Objective

This study aimed to identify psychological, behavioural, relational, and contextual factors associated with online grooming victimisation in adolescents and to explore how these vulnerabilities vary across developmental stages, informing prevention strategies.

Participants and setting

Data were collected from 240 Portuguese adolescents aged 12-19 in schools in Porto, Portugal.

Methods

A quantitative cross-sectional design was used. Online grooming victimisation was coded as a dichotomous outcome based on reported grooming-related experiences. Individual, relational, behavioural, and victimisation factors were analysed. Descriptive analyses, group comparisons, and binary logistic regression models were conducted for the overall sample and separately by developmental group.

Results

Three predictors of online grooming victimisation emerged: risky online behaviours (OR = 1.21; 95% CI[1.10, 1.33]; p < .001), gender (OR = 2.49; 95% CI[1.22, 5.06]; p = .012), and (cyber)bullying (OR = 2.21; 95% CI[1.19, 4.10]; p = .012). Age-stratified models showed developmentally contingent vulnerability: early adolescence involved behavioural exposure, experiences of (cyber)bullying, and gendered vulnerability, whereas in later adolescence, risk was associated with risky online behaviours.

Conclusions

Prevention should adopt age-sensitive approaches addressing behavioural exposure, victimisation, and gendered vulnerability.

GDC-RR-bb9c3b722c.title: Faculty Perspectives on a Pre-Implementation Master’s Curriculum in Pediatric Occupational Therapy in Saudi Arabia: A qualitative study
GDC-RR-bb9c3b722c.abstract: Background Children with developmental disabilities in Saudi Arabia (SA) are increasingly in need of specialised rehabilitation, yet the occupational therapists trained to serve them remain in short supply. Despite a steady expansion of undergraduate occupational therapy programmes since 2010, no postgraduate programme in pediatric occupational therapy exists anywhere in SA. To address this gap, a Master’s programme in Pediatric Occupational Therapy (MPOT) was developed using the Kern Six-Step curriculum development framework. Before its first cohort could begin, a systematic faculty evaluation was conducted to assess the curriculum’s strengths, surface potential gaps, and gather expert recommendations. Methods A qualitative descriptive study was conducted in SA. Twelve faculty members and medical educators with backgrounds spanning occupational therapy, rehabilitation sciences, psychiatry, neurology, and medical education, drawn from SA and internationally were recruited through purposive sampling. Each participant reviewed the full curriculum document and submitted a written narrative evaluation responding to six open-ended questions. Data were analysed using Braun and Clarke’s six-phase thematic analysis framework. Ethical approval was granted by King Abduallah International Medical Research Center. Results Eight themes emerged from the analysis: alignment with national healthcare priorities and workforce needs; content breadth and pediatric specialisation; curriculum coherence, structure, and academic rigour; teaching and learning effectiveness; quality assurance and standards alignment; research orientation and scholarly development; identified gaps and areas for improvement; and forward-looking recommendations. Participants strongly endorsed the curriculum’s national relevance, depth of pediatric specialisation, and alignment with World Federation of Occupational Therapy standards. Recurring concerns centred on limited clinical practicum structure, assessment transparency, workload feasibility for working clinicians, and insufficient coverage of interprofessional education and emerging digital health competencies. Conclusion This pre-implementation evaluation affirms the MPOT curriculum’s promise as a meaningful response to a critical workforce gap in SA. Beyond its local relevance, the study offers a replicable model for prospective curriculum evaluation in allied health postgraduate education one that other institutions across the region and beyond may find instructive.

GDC-RR-a09e752631.title: Out-of-school children in Pakistan: a structured narrative review of determinants, interventions, and research trends from 1987 to 2025
GDC-RR-a09e752631.journal: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
GDC-RR-a09e752631.abstract: Purpose This structured narrative review examines research on out-of-school children (OOSC) in Pakistan from 1987 to 2025, focusing on the determinants of educational exclusion, intervention and policy responses, and the evolution of the research evidence. Design/methodology/approach Following a structured review approach informed by Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020 reporting principles, relevant literature was identified through searches of Education Resources Information Center, Journal Storage, Scopus, Google Scholar, PubMed, Taylor & Francis Online, SpringerLink and SAGE Journals, supplemented by reference-list screening and institutional sources. Thirty-two studies met the predefined inclusion criteria. Evidence was synthesized using an integrated narrative and thematic approach, while methodological appraisal was undertaken using design-appropriate Critical Appraisal Skills Programme, Joanna Briggs Institute and Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool frameworks, with documentary/conceptual appraisal used for desk-based, comparative and policy-oriented sources. Findings The review identifies poverty, limited parental education, child labor, gender norms, school distance, inadequate infrastructure and weak policy implementation as recurring determinants of educational exclusion. Girls, children with disabilities, working children, street-connected children and children in rural or underserved areas experience intersecting and compounded barriers. Intervention evidence remains limited and context-specific. Included studies provide evidence on girls' stipend programs, public–private education provision, community-oriented and non-formal approaches, and inclusive education; however, evidence regarding sustained effectiveness, scalability and long-term educational outcomes remains insufficient. The research landscape has also shifted from predominantly descriptive accounts of access towards more intersectional, policy-oriented and Sustainable Development Goal 4-aligned analyses. Important gaps remain in longitudinal evaluation, disability inclusion, migration, street-connected children and evidence from under-researched regions, particularly Balochistan and remote Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Originality/value This review integrates fragmented Pakistan-specific evidence on the structural, social, cultural, geographical and institutional processes shaping educational exclusion. By combining determinant-focused evidence with intervention and research-trend analysis, it provides a consolidated basis for context-sensitive policy development and identifies priorities for future research, implementation and monitoring.

GDC-RR-ef5edb0793.title: Digital Engagement Activities and Internet Adoption Among Chinese Older Adults: Roles of Family Relations and Personality Traits in China Family Panel Studies
GDC-RR-ef5edb0793.authors: Tang Y, Li B, Zhang J, Lin S.
GDC-RR-ef5edb0793.abstract: Objective To examine how personality traits and family factors (number of children, parent–child relationship) are associated with internet use among older adults in China, including adoption, weekly time online, and breadth of online functions used. Methods We analysed 2018 China Family Panel Studies (CFPS) data for adults aged ≥ 60 years (n = 8,003). Internet adoption (computer and/or mobile) was modelled with multivariable logistic regression. Weekly hours online and online functions used were modelled with OLS. Covariates included age, gender, education, urban residence, subjective social status, employment, and self-rated health. Results Internet adoption was higher with better education (OR = 2.05, 95% CI 1.91–2.20), urban residence (OR = 2.52, 2.07–3.07), openness (OR = 1.30, 1.17–1.43), and closer parent–child ties (OR = 1.15, 1.01–1.30); but lower with older age (OR = 0.93, 0.91–0.94), being employed (OR = 0.52, 0.43–0.63), more children (OR = 0.82, 0.75–0.91), and neuroticism (OR = 0.80, 0.71–0.90). Among internet users, weekly time online increased with openness (β = +1.90 hours/week) and education (β = +0.66 per schooling level) but decreased with conscientiousness (β = −1.66), current employment (β = −4.79), spousal presence (β = −2.63), number of children (β = −1.47 per child), and closer parent–child ties (β = −1.53 per point). Breadth of online functions increased with education (β = +0.27) and openness (β = +0.28) and decreased with number of children (β = −0.20). Conclusion Among Chinese older adults, openness consistently predicts deeper and broader internet engagement. More children and closer parent–child ties are linked to shorter use among users, even though better relationships facilitate initial adoption. Interventions tailored to personality (e.g., motivating less-open users) and targeting older adults with poor family ties could narrow digital divide.

GDC-RR-27e31bef5b.title: How Discrimination Shapes Care-Seeking for Black Caregivers of Children With Medical Complexity.
GDC-RR-27e31bef5b.authors: Nmoh A, Fish LJ, Rodriguez J, Moore C, Miles T, Powell L, Leach B, Baumgardner L, Makarushka C, Parnell HE, Parente V, White MJ.
GDC-RR-27e31bef5b.abstract:
Objectives

Black children with medical complexity (CMC) experience a disproportionately high number of hospitalizations and emergency department (ED) visits. This disparity may reflect systemic and interpersonal racism and discrimination. Understanding Black caregivers' experiences is essential to designing programs that reduce acute care use. This study described caregivers' experiences of racism and discrimination and explored how these experiences influence care-seeking and communication among Black caregivers of CMC.

Methods

In partnership with family advocacy organizations, we recruited Black caregivers of CMC via national advocacy groups, social media, and electronic health record messaging. Eligible caregivers had a child aged 0 to 21 years with a hospitalization or ED visit in the previous year and a score of 3 or more on the Children with Special Health Care Needs screener. Purposive sampling ensured that one-third of participants were from rural areas. Semistructured interviews, guided by Critical Race Theory, were recorded, transcribed, and analyzed thematically.

Results

Thirty-one caregivers completed interviews. Caregivers described discrimination in health care based on race and other characteristics. Five themes emerged in caregivers' experiences of racism: dismissal, stereotyping, fear of retaliation, dehumanization, and differential access to resources. These experiences contributed to distrust, caregiver burnout, and perceived negative health outcomes. Caregivers' responses to discrimination included withholding concerns, advocating, documenting, selecting specific clinicians, managing perceptions, and staying informed.

Conclusions

Perceived racism and discrimination shaped how Black caregivers of CMC communicated with clinicians and navigated health care, underscoring the need for health care systems and clinicians to foster trusting partnerships, address structural inequities, and provide equitable, family-centered care.

GDC-RR-85cc1a3be7.title: Myopia Frequency and Associated Factors Among Children and Adolescents Attending Tertiary Eye-Care Centers in Iraq: A Multicenter Study.
GDC-RR-85cc1a3be7.authors: Aljaberi HA, Rahmani S, Noori ZTM.
GDC-RR-85cc1a3be7.abstract:
Purpose

To quantify the frequency of myopia and examine demographic, behavioral, and ocular biometric correlates in a selected tertiary-care sample of Iraqi children and adolescents.

Methods

This retrospective, multicenter, cross-sectional comparative study included 6-18-year-olds examined during 2023-2025 at three tertiary eye care centers. Cycloplegic autorefraction and optical biometry were performed. Myopia was defined as right-eye spherical equivalent (SE) ≤-0.50 D. Multivariable logistic regression was used to evaluate factors associated with myopia, and linear regression was used to evaluate concurrent correlates of SE.

Results

Among 6,356 participants, 3,820 (60.1%) were myopic and 2,536 (39.9%) emmetropic. The frequency and severity of myopia increased with age. Axial length (AL) correlated strongly with SE (r = -0.80). Age (OR 1.18/year), parental myopia (OR 3.19), and urban residence (OR 1.16) were positively associated with myopia; outdoor exposure was inversely associated (OR 0.86/hour). Screen time showed an inverse adjusted association after a positive crude association. AL was the strongest concurrent biometric correlate of SE (-2.81 D/mm; R2 = 0.766).

Conclusion

The observed 60.1% myopia frequency applies to this selected tertiary-care sample and is not a population prevalence estimate for Iraqi youth. Older age, parental myopia, urban residence, and lower outdoor exposure were associated with myopia, while axial length was the strongest concurrent biometric correlate of SE.

GDC-RR-0d83664391.title: Determinants of prices of commercial electric breast pumps sold in Germany: a cross-sectional analysis
GDC-RR-0d83664391.authors: Gencel-Augusto, J.; Okanmelu, E.; Strobl, F.; Ziebart, M.; Theurich, M.
GDC-RR-0d83664391.abstract: In Germany, statutory health insurance covers the rental or purchase of breast pumps when a medical indication is present for the mother or infant, and a physician has issued a prescription. However, parents must pay out of pocket for commercially available breast pumps for returning to work or personal circumstances. High indirect costs for continuation of breastfeeding and direct costs for breast pumps and related equipment may pose substantial barriers to breastfeeding families, an issue relevant for health equity. To our knowledge, no studies have assessed the direct financial costs associated with the purchase of commercially available breast pumps. In this cross-sectional study, we examined digital marketplaces in Germany for commercial electric breast pumps between March 2025 and May 2026, across major online platforms. Our objective was to explore pump features that predict price. We identified 282 commercial electric pump models from 108 brands. Basic information was unavailable for half of surveyed breast pump brands. The median price for surveyed commercial electric pumps was 72.70 EUR (IQR: 82.70), with costs ranging widely from 19.99 to 659.57 EUR. Prices varied by marketplace, manufacturer location, accessories, pump system type, power source, battery capacity, flange sizes, availability of instruction manuals, and single user claims; predicting significantly higher costs. Half of pumps surveyed offered only one flange size, signaling additional expenses for mothers needing alternative sizes. These findings highlight important considerations for maternal health and consumer safety. Health technology assessments and a review of current health policy on reimbursement for commercial electric breast pumps is needed

GDC-RR-553f7dc067.title: Digital Encounters and Protection Pathways Across Adolescence: Age- and Gender-Related Patterns in 26,297 European Adolescents Digital encounters and protection pathways
GDC-RR-553f7dc067.authors: Peter L, Laugner E, Fegert JM, Köhler-Dauner F.
GDC-RR-553f7dc067.abstract: Background Adolescent digital wellbeing cannot be understood from screen time alone. Young people differ not only in how long they use digital media, but also in the content and interactions they encounter, how they appraise their own use, and how they respond to online challenges. We examined age- and gender-related patterns across these dimensions in a large European sample, with particular attention to reported protection and support pathways. Methods We conducted a descriptive secondary analysis of published weighted aggregate youth tabulations from Flash Eurobarometer FL579, including 26,297 adolescents aged 13–18 years across the 27 EU Member States. We examined EU27 estimates and subgroup estimates by gender and age (13–14, 15–16, and 17–18 years) and calculated absolute percentage-point differences. Because respondent-level data were unavailable, individual-level associations, adjusted models, statistical uncertainty for derived contrasts, and causal effects could not be assessed. Results Screen time of at least six hours was reported by 46% of adolescents on a typical weekend day and 25% on a school day. Compared with 13–14-year-olds, adolescents aged 17–18 years more often reported prolonged screen time and perceived their screen time (48% vs. 36%) and social-media time (47% vs. 33%) as too high. Difficult-to-recognize AI-generated content (39%) and false or misleading information (35%) were the most frequently reported online encounters. The largest age-group difference in protection strategies concerned talking to a parent, teacher, or another adult (32% among 13–14-year-olds vs. 18% among 17–18-year-olds), whereas reporting harmful content or accounts was more common in the oldest group (30% vs. 21%). Conclusions Digital experiences and reported protection pathways differed substantially across adolescent age groups. Older adolescents more often reported several challenging online encounters and independently initiated or platform-based protective actions, whereas younger adolescents more often reported turning to adults. These cross-sectional aggregate patterns cannot establish within-person developmental change or substitution between strategies. They nevertheless highlight a potential tension between increasing digital autonomy and continued access to trusted support. Prevention should strengthen adolescent agency without transferring responsibility for structurally produced online risks from platforms, institutions, and adults to young people themselves.

Asked what they do to protect their wellbeing there, 32 percent of 13 and 14 year olds said they talk to a parent, teacher or another adult. Among 17 and 18 year olds it was 18 percent.

claudeReview.oneBelief: The open door is something a parent builds early, in calm moments, before it is needed. Connection is the protection.
claudeReview.oneTakeaway: Tonight, while they are still young enough to say yes to it, tell your child: if a screen ever gives you that uh oh feeling, you can always come to me, and you will never be in trouble for telling me.
claudeReview.reviewBasis: Two things read in this run. First, the European Commission's published youth tables for Flash Eurobarometer 579, Impact of excessive screen time and social media on young people's mental health, downloaded from the official data portal (data.europa.eu dataset s3686_fl579_eng): volume AA (EU27, questions 11 and 12a) and volume B (EU27 by gender and age, questions 10, 11, 12a and 12c), fieldwork 30 March to 16 April 2026, weighted. Every cleared figure below was read in those official tables. Second, the full text of the preprint, version 1, from the Research Square PDF for DOI 10.21203/rs.3.rs-11441481/v1 (posted 17 November 2026, not peer reviewed): abstract, methods, results, tables 1 to 3, discussion, limitations and declarations. The companion preprint GDC-RR-34b3878324 stays on HOLD: its figures were approximations of merged subgroups; the figures here are the Commission's own published percentages, read directly.

claims.claim: The youth survey covered 26,297 young people aged 13 to 18 in the 27 EU member states, fieldwork 30 March to 16 April 2026.
claims.basis: Official tables, volume AA and B: base EU27 (All) 26,297 unweighted and weighted; fieldwork dates printed on every sheet.

claims.claim: Talking to a parent, teacher or another adult, as a way to protect wellbeing on social media, was chosen by 32 percent of 13 to 14 year olds, 28 percent of 15 to 16 year olds and 18 percent of 17 to 18 year olds.
claims.basis: Official volume B, question 11. Correct, but the base is young people who use social media on a typical school day (23,595 unweighted), not all 26,297; the answer groups parents with teachers and other adults; and it is one of several options that could all be chosen. The EU27 figure is 26 percent.

claims.claim: Reporting harmful content or accounts rose from 21 percent at 13 to 14 to 30 percent at 17 to 18, and taking breaks from 28 to 35 percent.
claims.basis: Official volume B, question 11, same base.

claims.claim: In the past three months, AI generated content that was hard to recognise was reported by 34 percent of 13 to 14 year olds and 47 percent of 17 to 18 year olds, and unwanted sexualised content by 14 and 23 percent.
claims.basis: Official volume B, question 10, same base. The question covers content seen or experienced, so it is exposure, not victimisation.

claims.claim: Teenagers stop talking to their parents as they get older.
claims.basis: Cross sectional: three different age groups at one moment, not the same young people followed. The authors say the pattern may reflect development, cumulative experience or cohort, and cannot show change within a person. The item also bundles parents with teachers and other adults.

claims.claim: Older teenagers who see more risk are the ones who do not seek adult help.
claims.basis: The tables are aggregates and cannot link answers within the same person. The authors call this a hypothesis, not a demonstrated mechanism.

claudeReview.urgency: Low to moderate. Bank it. The Commission data are from spring 2026 and the preprint was posted on 17 November, so it is current for some weeks.
claudeReview.evidenceConfidence: HIGH that the European Commission's tables say what is written here: every figure was read in the official weighted tables. MODERATE as evidence for the point being made: a large official survey, but cross sectional, self reported, multiple choice, EU only, and the adult option bundles parents with teachers and others.
limitations: Cross sectional. Age group differences are not change within the same young people and may partly reflect cohort.
Question 11 was asked only of young people who use social media on a typical school day.
The option is talk to a parent, teacher or another adult, so parents cannot be separated out.
Multiple answers were allowed and the question does not measure how often, when, or whether it helped.
EU 27 only. The UK was not surveyed.
The analysis paper is a preprint and not peer reviewed, though the figures used here come from the Commission's own tables.
A finding that flatters our thesis, connection is the protection, so it was checked against the primary tables rather than taken from the preprint.

GDC-RR-c4dc6c4532.title: Low-dose atropine (0.01%) and visual discomfort: A clinic-based cohort linking pupil metrics, lighting context, and symptomatology in myopia control.
GDC-RR-c4dc6c4532.authors: Charan LS, Mahaur V, Tripathi H.
GDC-RR-c4dc6c4532.abstract: Low-dose atropine (0.01%) is widely used for pediatric myopia control, yet its effect on light-related visual discomfort under real-world lighting remains uncertain. We assembled a clinic-based observational cohort of 120 adolescents (12-18 years; myopia -3.00 to -6.00 D spherical equivalent) and compared 69 atropine users with 51 non-atropine controls. The primary outcome was a validated 0-10 visual discomfort composite score (Visual Discomfort Scale, VDS-10), administered under standardized ambient conditions (300 lx, 5000 K), with secondary measures including glare threshold (cd/m<sup>2</sup>; C-Quant, Oculus GmbH), pattern-glare score (Wilkins/Evans protocol), photopic and mesopic pupil diameters (PLR-200, NeurOptics), reading speed, and ambient lighting logged via wearable spectroradiometric sensors (Sekonic C-800). Multivariable ordinary least squares (OLS) models with HC3 robust standard errors and inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) adjusted for age, sex, screen-time, pupil metrics, illuminance, and correlated color temperature (CCT). Unadjusted means showed lower discomfort with atropine (mean 3.56 vs 4.67; mean difference - 1.12). Adjusted OLS yielded a non-significant atropine coefficient (β = 0.82; 95% CI -2.23 to 3.87; p = 0.598), while IPTW indicated a significant reduction (β ≈ -1.00; 95% CI -1.51 to -0.49; p < 0.001). A significant Atropine×CCT interaction indicated greater discomfort attenuation at higher CCT among atropine users; Atropine×Illuminance was not significant. Secondary outcomes showed no group differences in glare threshold, pattern-glare, pupil diameters, or reading speed. These findings indicate that 0.01% atropine does not increase visual discomfort and may confer a modest protective effect modulated by spectral characteristics of ambient lighting.

GDC-RR-1fadf51358.title: The relationship between digital creative aesthetic education and children’s emotional competence and social adaptation: a retrospective cohort study
GDC-RR-1fadf51358.abstract: Background Digital technology empowering aesthetic education has emerged as a novel preventive educational intervention in schools for promoting children’s mental health. The purpose of this study is to investigate the relationship between digital creative aesthetic education and children’s emotional competence and social adaptation, and to examine the potential mediating role of emotional competence in this relationship. Methods A retrospective cohort study was conducted using archived data, with 286 children enrolled. Participants were divided into an intervention group (148 children) and a control group (138 children) based on their participation in the digital creative aesthetic education intervention. The Emotional Skills and Competence Questionnaire for Children (ESCQ-C) was adopted to assess emotional competence. The Ages &amp; Stages Questionnaires: Social–Emotional, Second Edition (ASQ:SE-2) and Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales, Second Edition (VABS-II) were used to evaluate the level of social adaptation. Propensity score matching (PSM) was applied to balance confounding variables across groups. Repeated-measures analysis of variance (reporting the group × time interaction effect), multiple hierarchical regression and Bootstrap indirect effect tests were performed. Effect sizes were quantified using Cohen’s d, adjusted coefficient of determination (R 2 ), and bias-corrected 95% confidence intervals. Results The total score for emotional competence and scores on the emotion perception and management subdimensions were significantly higher in the intervention group than in the control group ( F = 23.614, p &lt; 0.001, Cohen’s d = 0.82). Children’s social adaptation scores improved significantly (ΔM = 12.36, SE = 2.15, p &lt; 0.001). Following PSM matching, the standardized mean difference of baseline variables in each group was below 10%, indicating satisfactory baseline balance between groups. Regression analysis indicated that digital creative aesthetic education positively and significantly predicted children’s emotional competence and social adaptation (adjusted R 2 = 0.317), and emotional competence may play a partial indirect role in the association between the two, with the indirect effect accounting for 28.47% of the total effect. Conclusion Children receiving digital creative aesthetic education showed better emotional competence and social adaptation than controls, which suggests its potential application value in advancing children’s health. This finding is derived from a retrospective observational design and requires further verification through prospective randomized controlled trials.

GDC-RR-df7c0a9f73.title: Global approaches to identifying pediatric hearing loss: a systematic scoping review of screening programs for preschool- and school-aged children
GDC-RR-df7c0a9f73.authors: Anna Grace Chang, Mahmoud Bassiony, Carolina Der, Shelly Chadha, Lauren K. Dillard
GDC-RR-df7c0a9f73.abstract: Introduction Hearing loss among children poses an important global health challenge. Hearing loss can have negative impacts throughout the life course and disproportionally impacts children residing in low- and middle-income countries. Systematic hearing screening among preschool- and school-aged children is a critical strategy in promoting the early identification and management of childhood hearing loss. The purpose of this scoping review is to provide a contemporary overview of global hearing screening approaches among preschool- and school-aged children. Materials and methods We searched PubMed, Ovid MEDLINE, and Scopus for studies focused on hearing screening among preschool- or school-aged children. Data regarding screening protocols, equipment, etiologies of identified hearing loss, and follow-up were qualitatively synthesized. All review processes were performed by two independent reviewers. Results Sixty-five original research articles from 30 countries (out of 194 member states) and across all six WHO regions were included in this scoping review. Commonly reported etiologies of hearing loss included addressable causes, such as cerumen impaction and otitis media, or other middle ear disease. While pure-tone audiometry remained the most common screening tool (used in 92.3% of studies), otoscopy and otoacoustic emissions (OAEs) were also widely used. Moreover, we identified 18 studies utilizing mobile phone or tablet applications and two employing telehealth-based approaches to screen for hearing loss, highlighting a shift toward use of low-cost technology in resource-limited settings. Screening failure rates varied widely (1.2%–49.2%), and diagnostic follow-up rates were inconsistent (10%–100%), often hindered by parental perceptions and access barriers. True prevalence estimates of hearing loss were limited by inconsistency of follow-up diagnostic testing. Few guidelines for systematic hearing screening were identified and compliance with existing recommendations is limited. Discussion Significant heterogeneity persists in global hearing screening among preschool- and school-aged children. This highlights global challenges in implementation, adaptation, and standardization of hearing screening programs. Systematic review registration The protocol for this review is registered in Open Science Framework (registration: osf.io/whky8/ ).
