GDC-RR-0e448e575c.title: Effectiveness of Digital Interventions for Youth Anxiety, Depression, ADHD, and Misconduct: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
GDC-RR-0e448e575c.authors: Steinberg JS, Sun J, Venturo-Conerly KE, Cabrera K, Corn A, Eschtruth M, Khurana S, Kim MY, Mehringer E, Sood G, Spitzer M, Ugueto AM, Weisz JR
GDC-RR-0e448e575c.abstract: Meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) testing youth digital mental health interventions (DMHIs) typically evaluate one type of DMHI for one problem (e.g., computerized-CBT for depression); although DMHIs are diverse, few evaluations have examined a broad range of them to identify cross-cutting features associated with effectiveness. Searching PsycINFO and PubMed for RCTs testing DMHIs for pediatric anxiety, depression, ADHD, and/or misconduct, we identified 91 articles (35 testing ADHD interventions, anxiety = 29, depression = 14, misconduct = 8, multiple = 5 [102 treatment-control comparisons]). Robust variance estimation (RVE) analyses demonstrated pooled effect sizes (ES) of g = 0.29 (95% CI [0.24, 0.35], p < .001) at post-treatment and g = 0.21 (95% CI [0.12, 0.30], p < .001) at follow-up, with substantial between-study heterogeneity at post-treatment (I<sup>2</sup> = 49.15%; τ<sup>2</sup> = 0.05; 95% PI [-0.15, 0.74]) and follow-up (I<sup>2</sup> = 54.96%; τ<sup>2</sup> = 0.05; 95% PI [-0.25, 0.67]). We conducted bivariate moderator analyses (e.g., intervention target, content, administration method) and covariate-adjusted models. Sources of between-study heterogeneity include treatment type (e.g., larger effects for CBT than bio-/neurofeedback), therapist support (larger effects with vs. without), and control group (larger effects when compared against no-treatment controls vs. active controls). Treatment target also moderated ES (e.g., anxiety [g = 0.41] greater than ADHD [g = 0.16]). Future work should attend to publication and study-quality-related bias, and test promising DMHI features experimentally.PROSPERO Pre-Registration: CRD42022357707 ( https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD42022357707 ).

GDC-RR-9320b06a2d.title: PraBat: An item response theory-based test battery to assess individual differences in pragmatic abilities in preschool children from different cultural backgrounds
GDC-RR-9320b06a2d.authors: Carraro C, Waffen P, Küçükerdoğan P, Yiğit EA, Odedra MJ, Zeidler H, Küntay AC, Koymen B, Haun D, Bohn M.
GDC-RR-9320b06a2d.abstract: Pragmatic abilities allow us to use and comprehend language in interaction. The assessment of individual differences in pragmatic abilities, both within and across cultural settings, is crucial to understanding how they develop. However, tools with good psychometric properties that suit this purpose are lacking. The current study describes the creation of a test battery assessing individual differences in 3- to 6-year-old children from different cultural and linguistic backgrounds. The battery is implemented as a tablet-based game, administrable both online and in person. Children are prompted by a character with one or multiple utterances and respond by selecting a picture among three options on a screen. An initial larger item pool was piloted in Germany and Kenya to ensure the items’ cross-cultural adaptability. We then used item response modeling on a sample of 713 German children to select items that varied in difficulty and fit the Rasch model. The so-constructed 19-item battery shows excellent model fit, test-retest reliability and convergent validity. The way the battery was created allows for easy cross-cultural adaptation, easy administration and scoring, thereby addressing an important gap in the developmental study of the interplay between social cognition and language. All materials and code are freely accessible to interested researchers. The task can be used via the following website: https://devpsy.web.leuphana.de/prabat/.

GDC-RR-ebb341e607.title: Quality standards in child-to-parent violence prevention programs: evidence from Spain
GDC-RR-ebb341e607.authors: Victoria Hidalgo, Bárbara Lorence, Sofía Baena, Shirley Arias-Rivera
GDC-RR-ebb341e607.abstract: Child-to-parent violence (CPV) represents a multi-causal phenomenon that has become a major social concern due to its steady increase in recent years. In Spain, official judicial records indicate that more than 4,500 cases of child-to-parent violence involving minors were recorded in 2024. However, multiple reports suggest that these figures represent only the most severe cases, as it is estimated that merely 10%–15% of incidents are formally reported. Given this situation, a coordinated and integrated response from professionals, academics, policymakers, and society at large is required in order to address the problem effectively. This study aimed to identify prevention programs currently implemented in Spain to address child-to-parent violence and to examine their characteristics, evidence-based quality indicators, and key intervention components. The search for CPV prevention and intervention programs involved a combination of strategies, including general online searches, targeted searches of specific webpages and repositories, a review of scientific literature, and consultation with experts. A total of 29 prevention and programs were identified, three of which were not being implemented at the time of data collection. Most programs were implemented within the justice system and primarily targeted indicated and selective population, with a smaller proportion focused on universal prevention. Most interventions targeted both adolescents and parents, and were delivered in an individual modality, although 64.29% also incorporated a group-based component. Regarding implementation and evaluation, most programs provided general guidelines or orientations but lacked a fully manualized intervention. In addition, while most programs included some form of internal evaluation, these evaluations were generally not publicly available or published. These findings indicate that Spain has a relevant number of programs targeting CPV, particularly from the justice system and social services, highlighting the need for more universal prevention actions. Although most programs included evaluations and orientation guidelines, the limited degree of manualization and the scarcity of systematic, publicly available evaluations hinder the assessment of their effectiveness and replicability. Strengthening quality standards through the development of evidence-based manuals, including change mechanisms and theoretical frameworks, and rigorous evaluation frameworks, promoting the collaborating between research and practice, could enhance the consistency and overall impact of CPV interventions in Spain.

GDC-RR-74a960dc7f.title: A Digital Intervention Reduces Childhood Obesity Risk Behaviors: Analysis of Secondary Outcomes of the Greenlight Plus RCT.
GDC-RR-74a960dc7f.authors: Wood CT, Perrin EM, Kay MC, Bian A, Schildcrout JS, Heerman WJ, Yin HS, Rothman RL, Flower KB, Sanders L, Adams LE, Delamater AM
GDC-RR-74a960dc7f.abstract:
Objective

This study examined key behavioral outcomes from the Greenlight Plus RCT.

Methods

Greenlight Plus was a comparative effectiveness trial from birth to 2 years of life that enrolled 900 dyads from October 2019 through January 2022 across six US medical centers. The clinic-only group received counseling at visits, and the clinic + digital group received tailored, responsive text messages. We assessed 14 parent-reported behaviors selected a priori. We tested overall effects, then estimated individual outcome intervention effects with logistic regression and proportional odds logistic regression models.

Results

We analyzed 857 dyads (424 in the clinic + digital group and 433 in the clinic-only group) and found a significant effect on behaviors overall (Χ2 = 40.54, df = 14, p = 0.0002), including greater breastfeeding at 6 months (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.46, 95% CI: 1.02, 2.10), lower sugar-sweetened beverage consumption at 9 (aOR 0.60, 95% CI: 0.40, 0.90) and 12 months (aOR 0.58, 95% CI: 0.40, 0.86), lower screen time at 9 (aOR 0.59, 95% CI: 0.45, 0.79) and 15 months (aOR 0.61, 95% CI: 0.45, 0.82), and more "tummy time" at 4 months (aOR 1.46, 95% CI: 1.12, 1.92).

Conclusions

The Greenlight Plus intervention led to significant improvements in breastfeeding, sugar-sweetened beverage consumption, screen time, and tummy time.

Trial registration

ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT04042467.

GDC-RR-62fd619e21.title: Justice-involved young people who reside in secure children’s homes: staff experiences of the impact of trauma on relationships
GDC-RR-62fd619e21.authors: Leanne Taylor, Elizabeth Wakeland, Suzanne Wheeler
GDC-RR-62fd619e21.abstract: Purpose The purpose of this study is to examine the experiences of staff working in secure children’s homes (SCHs) with justice-involved young people who have experienced trauma, and the impact of this has on the staff-young person relationship. Design/methodology/approach Four participants were interviewed through semi-structured means about their experiences. Results were recorded and transcribed. Analysis was undertaken using Interpretive Phenomenological Analysis. Findings Six group experiential themes were identified: “An Uphill Struggle”, Young People Use Safety Strategies, Building Predictability to Combat Chaos, Being Child-Focused to Overcome Challenges, Relationships are a Blueprint and Challenges of the Role. Subthemes were identified in four of the group experiential themes. Research limitations/implications The sample was limited to four participants, which is not representative of all SCHs and staff. However, it provides unique insight. The social media advert may evoke participation bias. Future research would benefit from exploring this from the young person’s perspective. Practical implications Implementation of trauma-informed frameworks are beneficial to promote greater outcomes for young people and support for staff. Social implications Greater understanding on the impact on trauma on relationships may foster more positive relationships with young people in SCHs. It may also facilitate support networks for staff. Originality/value To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this is the first study to explore staff experiences of how trauma impacts on relationships in SCHs.

GDC-RR-4f2225af95.title: Media Affordances and Pedagogical Quality of Indonesian Educational Apps for Young Children
GDC-RR-4f2225af95.journal: Ganaya : Jurnal Ilmu Sosial dan Humaniora
GDC-RR-4f2225af95.authors: Puri Bestari Mardani, Maria Febiana Christanti, Rut Rismanta Silalahi
GDC-RR-4f2225af95.abstract: Indonesia’s Government Regulation on Child Protection in Electronic Systems (PP Tunas) restricts children’s access to eight digital platforms, yet families lack evidence on which digital learning alternatives suit young children. This study aims to describe the pedagogical and communication affordance profiles of three selected Indonesian-language educational apps, namely Marbel Kids, Solite Kids, and Smarttick Indonesia, and to discuss their viability as alternatives under PP Tunas. A descriptive evaluative design was used. Apps were identified through a purposive, non-systematic search of app stores, assessed by the researchers through structured simulations using a 0–3 ordinal rubric that combines Media Affordance Theory with the Four Pillars of Learning, and complemented by naturalistic observations of four children aged 3–5 years. The results show different affordance profiles. Marbel Kids obtained the highest unweighted score (9/12), with strengths in ad-free engagement and contextual learning. Solite Kids (7/12) offered the broadest cultural and socio-moral content and the most affordable access, but advertising at feature transitions weakened engagement. Smarttick Indonesia (6/12) offered the greatest depth in structured mathematics, but its content was narrow and its design excluded parents during sessions. Social affordances supporting parent–child co-engagement were the least developed dimension in all three apps. The scores are descriptive heuristics, not measures of absolute quality. In conclusion, each app suits a different niche and none fully meets all dimensions of PP Tunas, so active parental mediation and a complementary combination of apps are needed. These preliminary findings require validation with a broader sample of apps.

GDC-RR-1f4ddcb76f.title: A Social Media Mining and Questionnaire Survey Hybrid Approach to Characterizing Caregiver Knowledge, Attitudes, and Practices on House Dust Mite Control: Cross-Sectional Study.
GDC-RR-1f4ddcb76f.authors: Yang P, Xian R, Li J, Zhao J, Xie H, Jiang Z, Hu Y, Xu X, Zang N, Zhao Y, Fang H, Liu E.
GDC-RR-1f4ddcb76f.abstract:
Background

House dust mite (HDM) sensitization commonly begins in early life and contributes to persistent allergic airway inflammation and asthma chronicity. Primary prevention via early-life environmental control is a potential pathway to reduce HDM sensitization and asthma risk.

Objective

This study aims to characterize child caregivers' knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP) regarding pediatric HDM control using a hybrid literature/expert-driven and social media-driven approach and to examine associations between KAP levels, child age, and caregiver HDM-related online engagement.

Methods

This cross-sectional study comprised two interconnected components: (1) mining of content published between August 2023 and July 2025 from 5 major Chinese social media platforms, analyzed via latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA), and (2) a social media-enhanced web-based KAP survey administered in November 2025 to child caregivers in Chongqing, China. In total, 132,341 social media documents and 2275 caregivers of children younger than 18 years were included in the analysis. The main outcomes included social media discourse patterns and domain-specific KAP levels across 5 dimensions: foundational knowledge (K1), recommended control knowledge (K2), attitude toward social media topics (A1), attitude toward recommended methods (A2), and control practices (P). Stratified analysis was conducted by 2 exposure variables: child age (≤3 years vs >3 years) and caregiver HDM-related online engagement (engaged vs nonengaged).

Results

LDA topic modeling identified 5 distinct topic clusters in the social media content. Commercial, emotional, and misleading content collectively dominated the information landscape, accounting for 83.3% (n=110,254) of the included documents (65.8% of the tokens), with commercial content often systematically conflating the concepts of "disinfection" and "mite elimination." Only 16.7% (n=22,087) of the documents (34.1% of the tokens) were classified as health educational content focusing on HDM allergy prevention, reflecting that this valid educational content is substantially longer and more information-dense than other social media posts. The average KAP levels of K1, K2, A1, A2, and P domains were 62.9%, 84.7%, 57.0%, 37.8%, and 25.8%, respectively. Social media emerged as the primary knowledge source (80.7%, n=1836), with methodological knowledge gaps (47.5%) being the top implementation barrier. Caregivers of children ≤3 years had significantly lower self-rated knowledge (23.5% vs 28.3%; P=.01), stronger endorsement of recommended methods, but also greater information overload (odds ratio [OR] 1.39, 95% CI 1.15-1.67; P<.001) and efficacy uncertainty (OR 1.23, 95% CI 1.01-1.52; P=.04). Caregivers with HDM-related online engagement showed better performance across multiple items in 5 domains, but also increased traditional practice with uncertain evidence (ultraviolet irradiation: OR 1.85, 95% CI 1.35-2.53; P<.001) and misconception acceptance (allergy impact exaggeration: OR 1.39, 95% CI 1.04-1.87; P=.03).

Conclusions

Complex and suboptimal KAP levels exist, particularly among caregivers of young children (≤3 years). HDM-related online engagement is associated with both enhanced implementation of control practices and elevated misconception endorsement. These findings reveal critical educational gaps and the necessity of social media intervention.

GDC-RR-ec57ce6ab6.title: The everyday ecology of children’s emotional experience
GDC-RR-ec57ce6ab6.authors: de Barbaro K, Jiang X, Maclaine BA, De La Torre Pinedo K, Croft A, Castillo AS, Vela M, Klinginsmith M, Jacobvitz D, Quiñones-Camacho L, Galhotra Y.
GDC-RR-ec57ce6ab6.abstract: Emotional experiences are fundamental inputs to human development, yet we know surprisingly little about their distribution in everyday life. Research typically characterizes children’s emotional environments using global reports or brief observations, obscuring the real-time contexts in which emotions arise. Here, we used artificial intelligence to automatically transcribe and annotate daylong audio recordings from three samples totaling N=159 families with children aged 5 months-8 years old (48.43% female). Our findings reveal the architecture of children’s everyday emotional environments: positive speech was concentrated during play and music, and 25% of speech segments conveyed frustration, concentrated during routine caregiving. Mothers’ mental health did not predict affective speech, but lower child effortful control predicted more frustration in our toddler sample. Frustration peaked in early toddlerhood, suggesting that children’s growing independence at this age may reorganize family emotional environments. Overall, emotional speech appears to emerge from everyday activity, with meaningful shifts across development.

GDC-RR-0383fb2e28.title: Who reports change? A PRISMA 2020 systematic review and stratified multi-informant meta-analysis of digital self-directed parenting programmes for children aged 2–12
GDC-RR-0383fb2e28.abstract:
Background: Self-directed digital parenting programmes are widely promoted for childhood disruptive behaviour, anxiety, and lifestyle risk, yet parents simultaneously receive the unmasked intervention and serve as primary proxy informants of child change. Pooling incompatible reporters obscures whether gains generalise beyond the participating caregiver.

Methods:

Under PRISMA 2020 guidelines, an archival register (8,047 records) and multi-database searches across OpenAlex, Crossref, Semantic Scholar, and Europe PMC/PubMed with Unpaywall resolution (2,493 records through 8 November 2026; 7,928 unique records screened) verified 144 full texts across 38 qualitative/audit cohorts and 27 unique RCT cohorts (28 non-overlapping contrasts; N = 10,157 randomised families; ages 2–12; 51 channel estimates). Subgroup A REML meta-analyses stratified six informant channels across superiority and active-comparator trials. Subgroup B synthesised within-trial paired contrasts (Δg = g_parent − g_second; 19 multi-informant cohorts, 22 pairs) across cross-reporter correlations (r = .20, .35, .50) and tested channel independence and denominator balance (N_second / N_parent).

Results:

In superiority RCTs (24 cohorts, 25 arms), unmasked parent ratings showed a robust benefit (k = 25, N = 7,412, g = +0.252, 95% CI [+0.187, +0.316], p = 1.84 × 10⁻¹⁴, I² = 54.7%), moderating from guided packages (g = +0.406) to purely self-directed programmes (k = 17, g = +0.211; Egger p = .0027; PEESE g = +0.143). Pooled independent non-parent channels yielded a null effect with zero heterogeneity (k = 12, N = 2,406 assessments across 11 cohorts [2,054 children], g = +0.023 [−0.051, +0.096], p = .545, I² = 0%): independent child self-report (k = 3, g = +0.037), teacher report (k = 2, g = −0.031), masked video observation (k = 3, g = +0.004), and wearable accelerometry/blinded anthropometry (k = 4, g = +0.014). Corroboration occurred only when secondary channels remained coupled to the unmasked parent via parent clinician interviews (k = 6, g = +0.419; pure self-directed k = 3, g = +0.212) or parent-forwarded child chat links (g = +0.401). Paired contrasts confirmed a superiority informant wedge (k = 11, Δg = +0.266 [+0.167, +0.364], p = 1.29 × 10⁻⁷ at r = .35; β₀ = +0.253 at N_S/N_P = 1.0; R² = 88.0%), reversing when staff delivery beat online self-help on parent ratings but not masked video (Δg = −0.414, p = .0028) or teacher ratings (Δg = −0.296, p = .024).

Conclusions:

Unmasked parent-reported child gains in self-directed digital programmes do not transfer to independent child, teacher, masked video, or sensor channels. Trials must separate informant channels, balance denominators, and report cross-reporter covariances.

GDC-RR-431ad60ca8.title: Feasibility, acceptability, and preliminary outcomes of blended modality online parent training in exposure and response-prevention (ERP) for children with OCD.
GDC-RR-431ad60ca8.authors: Scott S, Calteaux IG, Farrell LJ
GDC-RR-431ad60ca8.abstract:
Objective

This study evaluated the co-design, feasibility, acceptability, and preliminary outcomes of a brief, intensive, parent-led cognitive behavioural therapy with exposure and response prevention (CBT-ERP) intervention delivered via a blended digital modality.

Method

An open pilot case series (N = 4) involved families of children aged 7-14 years diagnosed with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). The intervention comprised four self-guided web-based modules, four therapist-led videoconference group sessions, and a three-week maintenance phase with brief therapist check-ins. Feasibility was assessed through adherence, acceptability through usability, satisfaction, and recommendation ratings, and preliminary outcomes through clinician-, parent-, and child-reported OCD severity. .

Results

Findings indicated high feasibility and acceptability, with strong intervention adherence and usability ratings within the "best imaginable" range. Parents reported high satisfaction, particularly with therapist-led sessions. OCD symptom severity decreased across measures, with 50% of participants no longer meeting diagnostic criteria at post-treatment, although changes were not statistically significant. Family accommodation remained relatively stable.

Conclusions

Findings provide preliminary support for the feasibility and acceptability of blended, parent-led CBT-ERP as a potentially scalable intervention for paediatric OCD. However, the small sample and uncontrolled design warrant cautious interpretation and further evaluation in larger controlled trials.

GDC-RR-d7f58f60c5.title: Knowledge, Attitudes and Self-reported Practices Regarding Special Educational Needs Among Medical Doctors Attending Online Continuing Professional Development Programmes in Sri Lanka: A Cross-Sectional Study
GDC-RR-d7f58f60c5.abstract: Background Doctors contribute to recognising and referring children with special educational needs (SEN), but evidence on their preparedness in Sri Lanka is limited. This study assessed knowledge, attitudes, self-reported practices and factors associated with good practice among doctors attending online continuing professional development (CPD) programmes. Methods A cross-sectional online survey was conducted among 334 consecutively recruited eligible doctors attending selected CPD programmes in Sri Lanka during August 2026 and 332 were analysed. An expert-reviewed, pretested questionnaire assessed knowledge, attitudes, self-reported practices and perceived barriers. Expert-defined thresholds of ≥ 80% of maximum domain scores classified good knowledge, favourable attitudes and good practice. Multivariable logistic regression with backward elimination examined factors associated with good self-reported practice. Results Among participants, 60.2% were female and 88.9% worked in secondary or tertiary hospitals. Good knowledge, favourable attitudes and good self-reported practice were identified in 262(78.9%), 51 (15.4%) and 128 (38.6%) doctors, respectively. Only 21.4% expressed confidence in identifying SEN and 21.1% in counselling parents. Reported barriers included lack of training (66.0%), time constraints (45.8%) and lack of knowledge (42.8%). Good knowledge (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.96; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.20–3.21) and previous management of a child with SEN (aOR 1.69; 95% CI 1.02–2.78) were associated with higher odds of good practice. Managing > 50 paediatric patients weekly (aOR 0.54; 95% CI 0.30–0.96) and not having received SEN training (aOR 0.60; 95% CI 0.36–0.98) were associated with lower odds. Conclusion Among doctors attending selected online CPD programmes, gaps in knowledge, attitudes and self-reported practice accompanied commonly reported training and service barriers. The findings support evaluating practical professional education, clearer referral pathways and supportive clinical workflows. Cross-sectional data and non-probability sampling limit causal interpretation and generalisability.

GDC-RR-4d059ea1ab.title: Perceived Health in Mothers of Children With Neuropsychiatric Conditions: The Role of PTSS From Child-Related Trauma.
GDC-RR-4d059ea1ab.journal: Journal of autism and developmental disorders
GDC-RR-4d059ea1ab.authors: Lahav Y, Shalev A, Gafter L.
GDC-RR-4d059ea1ab.abstract:
Purpose

Mothers raising children with neuropsychiatric conditions, such as autism or other mental health disorders, encounter unique caregiving challenges that can adversely affect their psychological and physical health. While research has documented poorer perceived health among these mothers and identified elevated posttraumatic stress symptoms (PTSS) related to their children's upbringing, no study has explored how PTSS specifically contributes to perceived health in this population.

Methods

This study aimed to address this gap by examining 635 mothers, including 169 mothers of children with autism or mental health disorders and 466 mothers of children without disabilities. Participants completed self-report measures online. Analyses included permutation-based ANCOVAs, correlation analyses, and hierarchical regression analyses.

Results

Results showed that mothers of children with autism or mental health disorders reported worse self-rated health (SRH), more somatic complaints, and a higher number of health problems compared to comparison mothers. PTSS was negatively associated with perceived health, while perceived social support was positively associated. However, regression analyses indicated that PTSS was a significant predictor of all three health indicators, independent of age, substance use, and perceived social support. After including PTSS in the regression models, the effect of perceived social support on SRH and somatic complaints became non-significant.

Conclusion

These findings underscore the role of posttraumatic distress from child-rearing trauma in shaping perceived health among mothers of children with neuropsychiatric conditions and underscores the need for trauma-focused interventions to mitigate the negative impact of PTSS on their health perceptions.

GDC-RR-d43d87dffd.title: Low-Cost Accessible Switch Kit for Age-Appropriate Play in Early Intervention: A Technical Report.
GDC-RR-d43d87dffd.journal: Pediatric physical therapy : the official publication of the Section on Pediatrics of the American Physical Therapy Association
GDC-RR-d43d87dffd.authors: Hoffman ME, Bokowy K, Bose A, Li T, Feldner HA, Steele KM.
GDC-RR-d43d87dffd.abstract:
Purpose

This report introduces Switch Kit, an open-source toolkit designed to make play accessible for children with disabilities.

Summary of key points

The Switch Kit consists of three components: (1) an input device that connects adaptive switches to tablets or computers, (2) age-appropriate, interactive media created in the easy-to-use Scratch coding language, and (3) guidelines for constructing low-cost switches from commonly available materials. The input device costs $70 to $75 to adapt, and switches can be made for under $6. All information is open source (https://miahoffmannd.github.io/switchkit/).

Conclusions and recommendations for clinical practice

The Switch Kit is a flexible, affordable option to integrate digital play into early intervention therapies. Customizable media can incorporate child-specific motivators, while multiple switch options allow clinicians to trial different setups and tailor solutions to individual needs. Applications range from simple cause-and-effect activities to multi-switch learning tasks, supporting engagement and participation.

GDC-RR-229062bda6.title: Barriers and Enablers to Accessing Sexual Health Services Among Underserved Communities: Community Organisations’ Perspectives on Sexual Health Inequalities
GDC-RR-229062bda6.authors: Farr R, Driscoll-Evans P, Pollock N, Dougall PDD, Reeves N, Wichterich H.
GDC-RR-229062bda6.abstract: Background Inequalities in access to sexual health services persist among underserved populations, with barriers shaped by intersecting structural, cultural and psychosocial factors. This study explored organisational perspectives on barriers and enablers to accessing sexual health services across Kent, with a particular focus on communities experiencing disadvantage and marginalisation. Methods An interpretivist qualitative design was adopted. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with representatives from 26 voluntary and community sector organisations supporting underserved populations across Kent. Interviews, conducted between May and June 2026, were informed by the Barriers and Enablers Framework and analysed thematically using the six-phase approach of Braun and Clarke. Additional qualitative evidence submitted by participating organisations was also considered. Results Participants identified multiple, intersecting barriers to equitable access, including limited appointment availability, clinic closures, poor transport, digital exclusion, competing life circumstances, uncertainty about confidentiality, stigma, cultural and language barriers, limited awareness and mistrust of statutory services. These barriers were particularly pronounced among ethnic minority and migrant communities, Gypsy, Roma and Traveller communities, people experiencing homelessness or substance use, LGBTQ+ communities, disabled people, young people and those affected by domestic abuse or contact with the criminal justice system. Community organisations were identified as important enablers through trusted relationships, practical support, culturally adapted communication, outreach and service navigation. Participants advocated flexible, community-based and co-produced models of care, supported by cross-sector collaboration, trauma-informed practice and community champions. Conclusion Equitable sexual health provision requires a shift beyond predominantly clinic-centred models towards flexible, culturally responsive and community-embedded approaches. Sustained investment in voluntary and community sector partnerships and meaningful co-production could strengthen accessibility, acceptability and engagement among underserved populations.

GDC-RR-f6929b2a6a.title: Financial Literacy and Digital Safety Education for Elementary School Students
GDC-RR-f6929b2a6a.authors: Ni Nyoman Reni Suasih, I Gusti Agung Ayu Apsari Anandari, Ida Ayu Gede Dyastari Saskara, Made Sinthya Aryasthini Mahaendrayasa, I Wayan Priyana Agus Sudharma, I Made Putra Yasa, Putu Ayu Dyandra Candra Putri, Agistiana Dewi
GDC-RR-f6929b2a6a.abstract: Financial literacy and digital safety are increasingly important for elementary school students as children are exposed to pocket money use, online games, cashless payments, mobile devices, and digital messages in daily life. This community service program aimed to strengthen students’ understanding of wise money management and safe digital behavior through interactive and child-friendly education. The activity was conducted at SD Negeri 1 Kemenuh, involving 52 students from grades 5 and 6. The learning materials covered basic financial literacy, including needs and wants, saving habits, and wise spending, as well as digital safety topics, including personal data protection, secret codes, and suspicious links. The program used storytelling, simple cases, games, quizzes, and short reflective prompts before and after the sessions. The results showed improvement in all evaluation indicators. Student understanding increased from 53.8% to 96.2% in identifying needs and wants, from 88.5% to 100.0% in saving habits, from 71.2% to 100.0% in wise spending, from 59.6% to 96.2% in secret code protection, and from 34.6% to 100.0% in recognizing suspicious links. These results indicate that integrated financial literacy and digital safety education can strengthen early economic awareness and safer digital behavior among elementary school students.

GDC-RR-04980f38d9.title: Multi-country RCT of a Systematically-Optimised, Remotely-Delivered Five-Session Parenting Intervention with Parents of Young Children with Conduct Problems.
GDC-RR-04980f38d9.authors: Heinrichs N, Lachman JM, Waller F, Müller J, Frantz I, Raleva M, Tăut D, Hutchings J, Gardner F, Ward CL, Fang X, Băban A, Lesco G, Babii V, Gajdadzis-Knezhevikj S, Foran HM.
GDC-RR-04980f38d9.abstract: Parenting programs are a recommended strategy to improve parenting skills and reduce disruptive behaviours but access to services is limited in North Macedonia, Republic of Moldova and Romania. We adapted a parenting program to this context, systematically optimized it and predicted positive change on child disruptive behaviours and several secondary domains compared to a lecture-only group. We conducted a multi-site randomized controlled trial of a remotely delivered group-based parenting intervention (5 sessions, n = 415 caregivers) against an online group lecture (1 session, n = 408 caregivers) in these three countries with 823 (primarily female) caregivers of children aged 2-9 years with elevated levels of behavioural difficulties (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT04721730, https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04721730). We randomized with a 1:1 ratio; partially masked outcome assessors, data analysts and 4 assessment points; pre: between 7 December 2020 and 17 May 2021, followed by program delivery with 4-month post-intervention assessment (25.0% dropout), and 12-month follow-up-assessment (35.0% dropout). Intention-to-treat analyses demonstrated small positive post-intervention effects on primary outcomes: reduced child aggressive behaviours (ß =0.15, SE = -1.40, p = .026, d = -0.30, 95% CI [-0.57, -0.04]), Oppositional Defiant Disorder/Conduct Disorder rates (4/135 [3.0%] vs. 5/112 [4.5%] in lecture group, rate ratio = 0.66, 95% CI [0.18, -2.46]), and a larger change in slope in the last 24-hour daily reports during intervention (p = .004, d = -0.37, 95% CI [-0.62, -0.11]). Primary outcome effects were not sustained at 12-month follow-up implying effort is needed to determine how to sustain effects longer-term of digitally delivered interventions in low resource contexts.

GDC-RR-79dd4d4260.title: Retinopathy of prematurity among infants in East Africa: a systematic review and Meta-analysis.
GDC-RR-79dd4d4260.authors: Ashebir YG, Getahun OK, Lakew G, Gemmechu MM, Zeleke ME, Atalay YA, Yirsaw AN, Bogale EK, Tikuneh AH, Hassen AA, Lake EA, Nigussie T, Bibi B, Jaleta FY, Belete AG, Getahun GK, Seid K, Jaleta CG, Lorato SS, Desalegn M, Rundasa DT.
GDC-RR-79dd4d4260.abstract:
Aim

To evaluate the pooled magnitude of retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) among infants' populations in East Africa.

Methods

A literature search was conducted using PubMed/MEDLINE, Google Scholar, Scopus, and African Journals Online to identify studies from East African published up to August 2025 that reported the magnitude of ROP and its associated factors. The quality of the included cohort and cross-sectional studies was assessed using a modified Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. A random-effects Meta-analysis was used to estimate the pooled magnitude of ROP and adjusted odds ratios (aORs) for associated factors, with results presented using 95% confidence intervals (CI). Heterogeneity among studies was assessed using the I² statistic, and subgroup analysis and meta-regression were performed to explore its sources. Publication bias was assessed using funnel plots and Egger's regression test.

Results

A total of 11 studies were included. The pooled magnitude of ROP in East Africa was 18% (95%CI: 13%-24%, I 2=95.77%). The Meta-analysis result showed that infants who received oxygen therapy (pooled OR=4.61, 95%CI: 1.88-7.33), neonates with birth weight less than 1500 g (pooled OR=5.82, 95%CI: 2.89-8.75), and respiratory distress syndrome (pooled OR=3.92, 95%CI: 2.54-5.29) were factors associated with ROP.

Conclusion

ROP is a significant public health concern in East Africa, affecting nearly one in five preterm infants. Policymakers and healthcare providers should prioritize evidence-based interventions targeting the prevention and early detection of ROP to mitigate its long-term impact on childhood blindness.

GDC-RR-428bdd9552.title: Electronic Screen Exposure and Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Systematic Review.
GDC-RR-428bdd9552.journal: Journal of autism and developmental disorders
GDC-RR-428bdd9552.abstract:
Purpose

This systematic review examined the association between early childhood electronic screen exposure and ASD or ASD-like characteristics in preschool children, whether reducing screen exposure changes those characteristics, and whether genetic/familial vulnerability moderates the association.

Methods

Nine databases were searched to December 2024. After screening 650 records, 11 studies (124,913 participants) met inclusion criteria. Quality was assessed using Kmet criteria. Given substantial heterogeneity in design, exposure definitions, outcomes, and reporting, findings were synthesized narratively without meta-analysis.

Results

Studies fell into three domains: (1) screen exposure and ASD-like characteristics; (2) screen reduction and changes in these characteristics; and (3) genetic/familial vulnerability as a moderator. Greater early screen exposure was frequently associated with ASD-like characteristics and related developmental concerns, including language and attentional difficulties. However, evidence was heterogeneous, and findings varied in quality and directness. Evidence on clinically diagnosed ASD was limited, and improvement after screen reduction rested mainly on uncontrolled case observations, often alongside increased caregiver-child interaction.

Conclusion

Evidence suggests an association between greater early screen exposure and ASD-like characteristics but does not establish that screen exposure causes ASD or that reducing it treats such characteristics. Confounding, reverse causation, caregiver-report bias, inconsistent measurement, and limited high-quality evidence restrict causal interpretation. "Virtual autism" and "Post-Digital Nannying Autism Syndrome" are not recognized diagnostic categories. Prospective longitudinal and quasi-experimental studies using standardized measures of content, context, timing, caregiver involvement, and outcomes are needed.

GDC-RR-bd0f80d94c.title: Social and family factors associated with the dual use of electronic cigarettes and tobacco in Spanish adolescents: a cross-sectional study
GDC-RR-bd0f80d94c.authors: Juan Antonio Clemente Soler, Juan Carlos Solano Lucas, Marcos Bote Díaz
GDC-RR-bd0f80d94c.abstract: Purpose This study aims to analyse the prevalence of lifetime and past-30-day exclusive and dual use of e-cigarettes and tobacco cigarettes among Spanish adolescents and to identify the social, family and socioeconomic factors associated with dual use. The study examines whether e-cigarette use displaces combustible tobacco or coexists with it within the same individuals and tests the role of peer and parental smoking, gender, parental employment status and self-perceived quality of information about substances, alongside psychosocial factors rarely considered in this literature, such as compulsive internet use, emotional distress and school motivation. Design/methodology/approach Cross-sectional survey of 1,105 adolescents aged 15–18 enrolled in secondary schools in the municipality of Murcia, Spain (2022–2023 academic year). A multistage stratified cluster design was applied, stratifying by educational level, school ownership and environment. Participation was 91.7% of schools and 98% of students. Data were collected anonymously through a self-administered questionnaire completed during class time. Current use followed the WHO 30-day criterion. Chi-square tests and a forward stepwise binary logistic regression restricted to current users (n = 410) contrasted dual use with exclusive use of either product (SPSS v.28). Findings Most adolescents had never used tobacco cigarettes (78.5%) or e-cigarettes (67.6%). Among the 410 current users, 14.9% used only tobacco cigarettes, 44.1% only e-cigarettes and 41.0% both products. In the adjusted model, dual use was associated with having friends who smoked (OR = 6.69; 95% CI: 3.8–11.8), having a mother who smoked (OR = 3.59; 1.9–6.7), being male (OR = 2.1; 1.2–3.6) and reporting being well informed about substance use (OR = 3.1; 1.2–8.0). Parental employment, emotional distress and compulsive internet use were not retained. Originality/value The study provides up-to-date evidence on dual nicotine use in a Southern European urban context, using a large representative adolescent sample. It tests parental employment status, an indicator seldom applied in adolescent vaping research and integrates psychosocial variables (compulsive internet use, emotional distress, school motivation) into models of dual use. The findings support the so-called information paradox and show that proximal social ties, rather than socioeconomic position, are the main correlates of dual use, informing family-oriented prevention, gender- and peer-sensitive school interventions and stricter regulation of minors’ access to e-cigarettes.

GDC-RR-2b2d33422a.title: National Trends and Demographic Disparities in Self-Reported Cognitive Difficulty Among U.S. High School Students, 2015-2023.
GDC-RR-2b2d33422a.journal: The Journal of school nursing : the official publication of the National Association of School Nurses
GDC-RR-2b2d33422a.authors: Nguyen AA, Jamal MM, Nguyen DL.
GDC-RR-2b2d33422a.abstract: The National Youth Risk Behavior Survey (YRBS) asks students whether, because of a physical, mental, or emotional problem, they have serious difficulty concentrating, remembering, or making decisions. We analyzed nationally representative 2015-2023 YRBS data from 50,222 U.S. high school students using survey-weighted prevalence estimates and logistic regression. The prevalence of this self-reported cognitive difficulty increased from 29.9% (95% CI, 27.7%-32.1%) in 2015 to 45.0% (95% CI, 43.1%-47.0%) in 2023-approximately 3 in 10 students to nearly 1 in 2 (adjusted odds ratio per 2-year cycle, 1.22; 95% CI, 1.18-1.25)-while 2021 and 2023 estimates were similar. The increase was steeper among female than male students. In secondary models, insufficient sleep, excessive recreational screen use, frequent poor mental health, household basic needs not consistently met, and unstable housing were associated with cognitive difficulty. These findings identify a growing functional signal requiring surveillance, school-health assessment, referral pathways, and further study.

GDC-RR-375dcc49b4.title: Physical activity in Swedish 3-year-old children: associations with lifestyle and behavioral factors
GDC-RR-375dcc49b4.authors: Ram Askeri, Richard Lundberg-Ulfsdotter, Daniel Jansson, Christina E. West, Jonas Sandlund, Wayne I. L. Davies, Katharina Wulff, Magnus Domellöf
GDC-RR-375dcc49b4.abstract: Abstract Background Physical activity (PA) positively affects children’s health and well-being. Despite numerous studies on factors that influence PA in adults and older school-children, limited information exists about lifestyle factors, behavior, and neurodevelopmental predictors of PA in preschool children. This study aimed to (i) quantify the time spent in various activity levels (vigorous, moderate, light, and sedentary) among 3-year-old Swedish children, and (ii) examine associations between actigraphy-measured PA and various lifestyle, behavioral factors, and health in this age group. Methods PA levels were measured using wrist-worn movement sensors (MotionWatch 8) in 497 3-year-old children in the ongoing NorthPop Birth Cohort in Northern Sweden. Motion data were collected over 24 h per day for eight continuous days and were classified into sleep, sedentary behavior, and PA intensities according to an age-, epoch-, and position-validated method. Children’s lifestyle, health, and demographic data were collected using register data and parental questionnaires. Neurodevelopment and behavior were assessed using the Ages & Stages Questionnaire (ASQ) and Strength and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ), respectively. Results Swedish 3-year-old children spent an average of 163 min on moderate-to-vigorous PA (MVPA) per day. Boys spent significantly more time at MVPA levels than girls ( p < 0.001). Children with better gross motor function, older siblings in the household, and spending more time playing outdoors demonstrated longer time spent at higher levels of PA over 24 h per day. Children with hyperactivity problems were more physically active, whereas those with peer problems had lower PA levels. Children who were exposed to more time playing on computer/phone spent less time being physically active. Conclusions Three-year-olds in Sweden are generally highly active, with nearly all (99%) meeting the WHO recommendation of at least 60 min of MVPA per day and all (100%) meeting the recommendation of at least 180 min of total daily physical activity. The explanatory factors associated with particular PA levels are multidimensional, but the results suggest that behaviors such as playing outdoors and spending less time playing on computers/phones are associated with higher PA levels in this age group. Clinical trial number Retrospectively registered at Researchweb 11 November 2024 (project number 279272).
grants: Umea University

GDC-RR-8973f0a40c.title: Engaging Educators and Children in Digital Play in Early Learning Settings
GDC-RR-8973f0a40c.authors: Patricia R. Collins, Fiona Boylan, Lennie Barblett, Pauline Roberts
GDC-RR-8973f0a40c.abstract: As digital technologies become increasingly embedded in early learning settings, educator guided play is gaining attention to enhance children’s purposeful, creative, and collaborative use of digital tools. This project upskilled three fourth-year preservice teachers as Digital Ambassadors (DAs), supporting educators to engage children in meaningful digital guided play experiences to support childrens computational thinking across three Early Childhood Education and Care (ECEC) settings. Guided by an interpretative paradigm, data were generated by both children and adults. Children wore GoPro cameras to capture their perspectives, while iPads on Swivl systems provided a broader view of interactions. Inductive and deductive analyses were conducted on video footage, play-based conversations, and reflections. Findings revealed children demonstrated digital knowledge and competencies beyond educator’s expectations, and that guided digital co-play fostered reciprocal learning, with adults learning alongside children. The study also raised critical questions about what constitutes meaningful digital play experiences in early childhood contexts.
grants: Edith Cowan University, School of Education

GDC-RR-540fff2c03.title: News, Politics, Societal Issues, and Hate on Youths’ Donated Social Media Feeds
GDC-RR-540fff2c03.authors: Oostrum K, Westera M, van den Bos W, Ma I.
GDC-RR-540fff2c03.abstract: Youth use social media as a main source for news, political, and societal information, raising urgent questions about the content of such news-like videos, such as the presence of hate speech. Characterizing their actual exposure to news-like content and hate speech requires innovative methods that are not dependent on subjective recall or synthetic accounts. Here, youth (16–25 years old) donated their TikTok feed histories spanning October 2023 till May 2026, resulting in ~6.7M public videos for our analyses. For each video, we extracted the transcripts, descriptions, hashtags, and viewing durations. We then used large-scale automated content classification with large language models (Llama 3.1-70B) to identify videos about news, politics, and major societal issues, such as climate change, migration, and war. We find that nearly all (98%) of the news-like content did not come from accounts that youth followed, suggesting that these were mostly algorithmic recommendations. The prevalence of news-like videos peaked during important political events such as elections. Only 13% originated from established news organizations present on TikTok. Instead, most of these videos came from niche content creators. These niche creators were more likely to produce hate speech videos in news-like content compared to other creators. Hate speech videos most often mentioned specific politicians, political parties, and minority groups. We cross checked the identified hate speech videoIDs with the EU transparency database and found that none were removed by the platform, suggesting inefficient content moderation. Our methods offer a scalable approach to directly measure youths’ exposure to social media content. This provides a foundation for investigating how digital information environments shape societal perceptions and attitudes during adolescence and emerging adulthood.

claudeReview.proposedTitle: Young people handed researchers their real TikTok feeds. Almost all the news and politics in them came from accounts they did not follow.
claudeReview.proposedAngle: The source is a preprint from Leiden University, posted on PsyArXiv on 18 November 2026 and not yet peer reviewed. 147 young people in the Netherlands aged 16 to 25, average age about 20, donated their TikTok feed histories, about 6.7 million public videos, mostly October 2023 to May 2026. For the typical person, 98 percent of that content came from accounts they did not follow, so it was most likely chosen for them by the recommendation system. Only about 13 percent came from established news organisations; most came from small niche creators, who were also the likeliest to post hateful videos. Our belief: teach the child how the feed works before they get it, so they arrive at sixteen knowing the recipe. Say once that our primary curriculum has a lesson, How algorithms work, whose glossary says of the feed: you do not choose it, the algorithm does. Close on one question for parents.

GDC-RR-7687a92150.title: How parents navigate toddler screen time under new recommendations: insights to inform digital intervention design
GDC-RR-7687a92150.authors: Segerros F, Hesketh KD, Löf M, Sandborg J.
GDC-RR-7687a92150.abstract: Background Although screen time recommendations for young children exist, most exceed recommended limits, and parents struggle to balance screen use in everyday life. Evidence on how parents of toddlers interpret recommendations and what support they find acceptable remains limited. Digital tools may offer scalable support, but understanding parental needs is essential for guiding design. This study aimed to examine how parents manage toddler screen time following the introduction of national recommendations, and to inform co-design of a digital support intervention. Methods Parents of 1-3-year-old children (n = 19) were recruited via preschools and child healthcare services in Sweden. Semi-structured interviews were conducted via video call between October 2024 and February 2026. The sample included both mothers (63%) and fathers (37%), predominantly highly educated, and both single- and multiple-child families. Interview transcripts were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. Results One overarching and three main themes were identified. Limiting screen use was framed as a marker of responsible and “good” parenting, reflecting moral expectations and parenting identity. Within this, parents navigated both their own and their child’s screen use within a shared digital environment, characterized by constant connectivity and competing everyday demands. While screen‑free time was seen as ideal, screen use was managed through ongoing, context‑dependent situational trade-offs. Recommendations were interpreted as flexible guidance rather than strict rules. They were used primarily as benchmarks for evaluating parenting rather than directing behavior and were perceived as lacking actionable, practical guidance. Instead, decisions about screen use were informed by personal experience, observations of others, and online and informal sources. Parents expressed a need for practical and context‑specific support, including guidance on managing everyday situations, regulating their own screen use, and translating recommendations into practice. Conclusions By examining parental management of toddler screen time following the introduction of national recommendations, this study highlights the need for actionable and context-specific support that complements existing time-based screen use guidance by addressing both parental and child screen use within everyday family contexts.

GDC-RR-cc9aa0f1d2.title: Designing a mHealth Intervention to Enhance Health, Nutrition, and Child Development for Urban Refugees and Host Communities in a Low-Resource Setting: Formative Qualitative Study.
GDC-RR-cc9aa0f1d2.authors: Marangu J, Abubakar A, Jensen N, Sibanda S, Tomlinson M.
GDC-RR-cc9aa0f1d2.abstract:
Background

Despite advances in addressing child health and undernutrition, low- and middle-income countries in Africa have experienced a persistently high number of children with suboptimal outcomes over the last decade. Caregivers of young children in low-resource settings have limited access to health and nutrition information to enhance child development. Digital interventions are a possible solution, although the factors for their success among urban, low-income refugee, and host communities are unclear.

Objective

This study explored the perceptions of health care workers and caregivers of health, nutrition, and early child development practices; identified barriers and facilitators for suitable digital interventions; and applied findings to a mobile health intervention design process.

Methods

We conducted a formative study to inform an intervention design using a qualitative approach. This involved key informant interviews (n=12) and 2 focus group discussions (n=17) with caregivers of children younger than 2 years. The key informants included health, nutrition, and child development officials from the Ministry of Health and representatives from community-based organizations. Data were analyzed using framework analysis.

Results

While there were some perceived positive practices among refugee and host communities, they were described by officials as being insufficient, especially regarding breastfeeding, dietary diversity, antenatal and postnatal care, and responsive caregiving. The availability of digital interventions was reported to be limited. Barriers such as limited access to smartphones and low digital literacy were seen as likely to hinder the uptake of digital interventions. However, use of existing resources such as community health promoters was seen as a facilitator of intervention uptake. The findings were mapped to intervention decision-making using the World Bank's Quality Framework for Parenting Programs, and content was informed by the Nurturing Care Framework.

Conclusions

The findings from this study contribute to our understanding of perceptions on health, nutrition, and child development within the context and are useful in informing important considerations for the design of a digital intervention to be tested in subsequent research.

GDC-RR-85d60e795a.title: Identity-based bullying and maladaptive weight control behaviors among sexual and gender minority youth: Does bullying subtype and format matter?
GDC-RR-85d60e795a.authors: Bennett BL, Lloyd KM, Puhl RM, Lamere A, Watson RJ.
GDC-RR-85d60e795a.abstract: Little is known about how bullying an individual because of their weight may be differentially associated with eating disorder risk compared to bullying for other identity components (e.g., gender, sexual orientation) among sexual and gender minority (SGM) youth. It is also unclear how bullying that occurs in-person versus online may impact maladaptive weight control behaviors. The present study quantified experiences of identity-based bullying and examined their differential associations with maladaptive weight control behaviors by subtype and setting (i.e., in school or online) of bullying. 12,868 adolescent participants who identified as SGM completed measures that assessed engagement in maladaptive weight control behaviors, and experiences of bullying in-school and online across domains of identity including weight, gender, race/ethnicity, sexual orientation, religion, disability, immigration status, and gender expression. High rates of bullying were documented across settings with it occurring more often in-person than online, t(12,152)=19.60, p<.001, d=.18. Experiencing bullying in either setting was associated with maladaptive weight control behaviors: bullying experiences in school, F(29, 10,240)=59.09, p<.001, R 2=.14 and bullying experiences online, F(29, 10,150)=50.25, p<.001, R 2=.13. There were slightly stronger associations between being bullied for visible components of identity (weight, gender expression, gender identity) and maladaptive weight control behaviors (βs=.23-.31 versus βs=.10-.25), though all types of bullying victimization across both settings were associated with greater engagement in these behaviors (p<.001 for all). These findings suggest that more resources are needed to combat bullying across locations and to facilitate coping for adolescents at increased risk of identity-based bullying.

GDC-RR-4924faefd3.title: Early intervention in children with fragile X syndrome: Prevalence, timing, and family perception.
GDC-RR-4924faefd3.authors: Dunajcik A, McDonald ER, Summers AD, Esler A, Gonzalez MG, Thompson-Paul AM, Schweizer M, Tinker SC, FORWARD Consortium.
GDC-RR-4924faefd3.abstract:
Objective

Fragile X syndrome (FXS) is a genetic disorder that commonly leads to intellectual and developmental delays and disabilities. Early intervention (EI) services and therapies provided to children under 3 years of age aim to improve developmental outcomes. This analysis examines the prevalence of EI receipt among children with FXS, enrollment timing, services used, and parental satisfaction with EI services.

Methods

Data were obtained from the Fragile X Online Registry With Accessible Research Database (FORWARD), collected from 2011 to 2021. Participants aged 3-21 years during at least one clinic visit were included. EI receipt and enrollment age were assessed overall and by demographic characteristics; services used and satisfaction with services were assessed in relation to EI enrollment age. All analyses were stratified by sex.

Results

Among 1114 participants, 86.0% of males and 59.6% of females received EI, with over 80% of parents reporting some level of satisfaction with services. EI receipt varied by household income, parental education, race/ethnicity, household language, and insurance. Among participants diagnosed with FXS at < 3 years, only 8.6% of males and 13.3% of females had a diagnosis before starting EI. Most EI participants received speech and language therapy (93.5% males, 90.3% females), occupational therapy (89.2% males, 72.4% females), and physical therapy (72.5% males, 50.3% females).

Conclusion

Most children began early intervention before FXS diagnosis, showing that EI receipt may depend more on recognition of developmental delays than genetic diagnosis. Parental satisfaction with EI was high, though receipt varied substantially by demographic factors, identifying opportunities for targeted outreach.

GDC-RR-a4e42698bb.title: Vulnerable Children in Nigeria: Classifications, Lived Conditions, and the Response Gap
GDC-RR-a4e42698bb.journal: Asian Research Journal of Arts & Social Sciences
GDC-RR-a4e42698bb.authors: Olafunmilayo A. Akinpelu, Jacob Olusola Odelola, Adisa Bolaji Iyanda
GDC-RR-a4e42698bb.abstract: Child vulnerability in Nigeria is documented through multiple surveys and service systems, but their estimates differ in population coverage, definitions and purposes. This narrative review synthesises Nigerian empirical studies, official statistics, policy documents and selected international literature across shelter, protection, health and education, using Oyo State and the South-West as illustrative contexts. Targeted online searches and source verification were completed in July 2026; national surveys were distinguished from local studies, programme reports and contextual news accounts. The 2022 national multidimensional poverty measure classified 67.5% of children aged 0–17 as poor, whereas the linked Child Multidimensional Poverty Index classified 83.5% of children aged 0–4 as poor; these indicators are not interchangeable. The 2022 child labour survey estimated 24.7 million children aged 5–17 in child labour, and education estimates based on the 2021 Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey identified approximately 17.8 million children aged 6–17 as out of school. Evidence also documents violence, barriers to care and psychological difficulties, although heterogeneous designs preclude a single contemporary vulnerability count or pooled trend. Existing instruments already include psychosocial and outcome indicators. The central measurement problem is therefore the incomplete integration of material conditions, service access and child-reported well-being, rather than their complete absence. Priorities include harmonised operational definitions, age-specific reporting, representative inclusion of marginalised groups, accountable referral systems and culturally appropriate longitudinal research. These measures would permit a clearer assessment of whether service provision accompanies sustained improvements in children's safety, functioning and lived experience.

GDC-RR-545a51df31.title: Body Image Health Promotion in Early Childhood: Randomised Controlled Trial of Body Blocks.
GDC-RR-545a51df31.journal: Health education & behavior : the official publication of the Society for Public Health Education
GDC-RR-545a51df31.authors: Radunz M, Norton L, Prichard I.
GDC-RR-545a51df31.abstract: Body image concerns represent a significant public health issue, with evidence of the desire for thinness beginning as early as the age of 6. Given early childhood educators play a crucial role in childhood development, there is a critical need for interventions that can increase educators' awareness and competency of promoting positive body image. This study addresses this gap by evaluating Body Blocks, an online programme for early childhood educators, on their knowledge, awareness, and competency in promoting positive body image. A randomised controlled trial was conducted with educators randomised to intervention or waitlist control. Fifty-eight early learning centres participated, with 31 centres (n = 111 educators; Mage = 39.54, SD = 11.44; 99.1% female) randomised to the intervention and 27 centres (n = 110 educators; Mage = 42.33, SD = 10.81; 99.1% female) randomised to waitlist control. Small effect size improvements were found relative to control at 1-week follow-up for knowledge (d =.38; 95% CI: .11, .65), awareness (d =.37; 95% CI: .13, .61) and competency (d =.21; 95% CI: .10, .32), with large improvements in educators' own body functionality appreciation (d = .71; 95% CI .44, .99). No significant effects were found across outcomes at 1-month follow-up. Overall, 70% of educators would recommend Body Blocks to others. Qualitative feedback demonstrated programme acceptability, with educators reporting more neutral language around food and bodies. Our findings highlight Body Blocks' potential as a scalable professional development tool. Future research should evaluate the effectiveness of supplementary materials in supporting educators' knowledge retention at 1-month follow-up.

GDC-RR-4635393f51.title: Gamification versus Conventional Oral Health Education on kindergarten Children’s Oral Hygiene in Al-Ahsa, Saudi Arabia: An experimental study
GDC-RR-4635393f51.authors: Alsuwayi HI, Nasir EF, Alomran AJ, Kassem AO, Suliman NMA.
GDC-RR-4635393f51.abstract: Background Oral hygiene in early childhood is a strong predictor of long-term dental health, yet conventional lecture-based education may be less engaging for preschoolers than interactive, game-based approaches. This study aimed to measure baseline oral hygiene status among preschool children in Al-Ahsa, Saudi Arabia, and to compare the effectiveness of non-conventional (game-based) versus conventional oral health education on children's oral hygiene outcomes. Materials and Methods A prospective, double-arm, single-blinded randomized controlled trial was conducted among preschool children aged 5–6 years enrolled in kindergartens across Al-Ahsa. Using stratified proportional sampling across three educational offices (Al-Hofuf, Al-Mubarraz, and Villages), 727 children (339 (Group A), and 328 (Group B) participated from thirteen kindergartens. Classes were randomly assigned to receive either a non-conventional program (interactive classroom sessions, online quiz games, and caregiver lectures) or a conventional PowerPoint-based lecture. Oral hygiene was assessed pre- and post-experiment using the Simplified Debris Index (DI-S) by a blinded examiner. Data were analyzed using chi-square tests, Welch's t-test, ANCOVA, Friedman and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, and non-parametric multivariable regression (rank-transform and median regression) to account for non-normal score distributions. Results The experiment (Group A) and control (Group B) were well balanced on sociodemographic characteristics, with minor differences in child age and residential distribution. Both groups showed statistically significant improvement in oral hygiene scores from pre- to post-experiment ( p < 0.001), with a very large effect in (Group A) compared to (Group B). Despite starting from a slightly worse baseline, (Group A) achieved significantly better post-experiment scores than (Group B), a difference that persisted after adjusting for baseline scores (ANCOVA: F (1,724) = 29.43, p < 0.001) and after further adjustment for sociodemographic covariates (median regression B = − 0.180, p < 0.001). Improvement was also more consistent in (Group A) (Kendall's W = 0.659) than (Group B) (W = 0.522). No sociodemographic variable was an independent predictor of post-experiment oral hygiene. Conclusion Both conventional and game-based oral health education significantly improved preschool children's oral hygiene, but the game-based, interactive approach produced greater and more consistent improvement, independent of sociodemographic factors. These findings support incorporating interactive, game-based methods into kindergarten oral health education programs. The study was retrospectively registered in the International Standard Randomized Controlled Trial on 23.10.2024, (registration number: ISRCTN71415867, https://www.isrctn.com/ISRCTN71415867).

GDC-RR-eb8c634ded.title: Optimizing dosing strategies for children with leprosy: A weight-banded dosing approach
GDC-RR-eb8c634ded.authors: van Dyk, J.; Masini, T.; Lambert, S. M.; Darlong, J.; Deps, P. D.; Nobre, M. L.; van Brakel, W.; Hill, B.; Timalsina, A. B.; Mane, S. S.; Malik, P.; Lal, V.; Wasmann, R. E.
GDC-RR-eb8c634ded.abstract: BackgroundDosing guidance for children with leprosy remains operationally challenging. For children under 10 years of age, current WHO recommendations rely on mg/kg dosing of the three separate components of leprosy multidrug therapy, which are difficult to implement in routine care and may result in inconsistent drug exposures. Weight-banded dosing offers a pragmatic alternative that better aligns with pharmacokinetic principles and existing drug formulations. MethodologyA pharmacokinetic simulation study was conducted to develop harmonized weight-banded dosing regimens for rifampicin, clofazimine, and dapsone in children aged 2 to <10 years. Using the WHO dosing tool, drug exposures across harmonized weight bands were simulated and adult-equivalent systemic exposure (80- 125% of adult area under the concentration-time curve) targeted. Predicted exposures were contextualized against safety reference regimens used in tuberculosis meningitis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, and leprosy. An iterative review process involving the WHO Technical Working Group on leprosy in children ensured clinical and operational feasibility. ResultsProposed weight-banded multidrug therapy regimens achieved adult-equivalent exposures across most weight bands. Predicted exposures modestly exceeded 125% of adult levels at the lower end of selected weight bands but remained well below safety benchmarks, namely exposures associated with daily rifampicin therapy for tuberculosis meningitis and clofazimine regimens for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis. Dapsone exposures were comparable to those achieved with current leprosy dosing. The existing 10-14-year-old child MDT blister pack could be used without modification in children weighing 25-39.9 kg and with limited tablet or gel capsule removal in children weighing 6-24.9 kg. ConclusionsA harmonized weight-banded dosing strategy was developed that enables effective, practical dosing of leprosy multidrug therapy in children under 10 years using existing free-of-charge blister packs provided through WHO. This approach improves dosing consistency, supports programmatic implementation, and provides a rational interim solution while child-friendly formulations are being developed. Author SummaryLeprosy continues to affect children in many low-resource settings, yet guidance on how to dose treatment in younger children remains limited. Current recommendations often require clinicians to calculate mg/kg doses, which can be difficult in practice and may not match the oral formulations that are available. In this study, we used computer-based simulations to develop a simplified dosing approach for the three drugs used to treat leprosy. We showed that grouping children into weight bands, rather than calculating individual doses, can achieve drug exposures similar to those seen in adults, where treatment is known to be effective. Importantly, we found that these doses can be delivered using existing pre-packed treatment kits by removing selected dose units, making this approach practical in routine care. This work provides a more straightforward and reliable way to treat children with leprosy, reducing the burden on clinicians and improving access to treatment. However, challenges remain, including the lack of child-friendly formulations and limited data on how these drugs behave in children. Further studies are needed to improve treatment for this vulnerable population.
